In the early part of the twenty-ninth year, Mr. Dai sent two telegrams, one after the other, directing the "Shanghai District" to set about organizing a "Shanghai Workers'-Movement Committee," and signifying his wish that the two brothers Liu Shaokui and Liu Junqing, who served in the "International Settlement police," should form its mainstay, with some notables of society invited besides to take part in the affair and lend it their name.

The first telegram was passed on by the "Shanghai District" to the two brothers Liu Shaokui and Liu Junqing; its gist was this: "Under present conditions, we should press forward the movement among the workmen of every trade in Shanghai, and keep in close touch with them, so as to strike at the very life of the enemy and the puppets. It is my thought that a 'Shanghai Workers'-Movement Committee' should at once be secretly organized; I beg you two brothers to make contact with the comrades in Shanghai and set about it with all speed. The needful funds shall be borne by the Center. The rest I beg you to settle in consultation with the comrades in Shanghai."

The second telegram was sent to the "Shanghai District"; its content ran: "The employment of the workers is of the first importance, for the secret-service work of today has need of many deep-laid lines and the cover of the common trades of society. It is my thought that a Workers'-Movement Committee should be organized, and I beg that the elder Yu Qia, Zhao Zigang, Liu Shaokui, Liu Junqing, and Jiang Futian, all these gentlemen, be its members; our Shanghai District may also choose and send men to take part in the work. Whatever monthly funds are needed shall be borne by the Center. The matter is pressing; I beg you, brother, to consult and set about it at once." (The writer's note: the telegram above was quoted once already in an earlier passage, to clear up how outsiders had come to misunderstand the venerable Mr. Yu Qiaqing, a report that ran wide of the truth.)

Judging from the tone of these two telegrams, and from the sentence twice repeated—"the funds needed shall be borne by the Center"—this work-project may well have sprung from some larger scheme, of which the part touching the "Shanghai workers' movement" was handed to the "Juntong Bureau" to carry out; whereupon, as a matter of course, the Bureau laid this charge in turn upon the "Shanghai District."

At the time this fairly stumped me, for I truly did not understand how a "workers' movement" ought to be run. I grasped well enough that secret-service work has need of many deep-laid lines and of occupational cover in every stratum of society; but to lead a workers' movement in secret, and, beyond that, to make it yield an auxiliary force against the enemy—that was no simple thing.

I always felt that a "workers' movement" ought to be led by the workers themselves, men who had not left off labor; an outsider could never take hold. Suppose one were to set men of the Concession police to the "workers' movement," and even to lead it—would that answer? For my own part I thought it not very fitting.

At that time, how many workers there were in all in the Shanghai region, within the Concessions and without, and how they were to be classed—for want of any statistics to go by, the writer can only say the word "unknown." Still, of that Greater Shanghai renowned as the first city of China—with its population of several millions and its hundred trades crowded together—one may suppose its working population must have been considerable indeed, its callings and crafts beyond all counting. If one leaned solely on those few gentlemen named in Mr. Dai's telegram to serve as workers'-committee members in name, and added to them the men the "Shanghai District" should pick out to take part, then—with no foundation whatever laid in the past—could the thing be got moving at all? It is not that I mean to throw cold water; look at it from any angle, and it would not do. To say a self-belittling word besides: neither in quality nor in quantity was there enough. By a rational reckoning, if it must be done, then first one would have to gather a band of men with connection, with knowledge, and with experience of this kind of work, plan it out well, and frame a whole method of going about it—then perhaps it might be worth a try; yet its success or failure would still hang upon whether the method was apt and whether the effort was made. This was no more than a private notion and view of my own, which I dared not openly send up above; that is to say, though in my heart I did not hold with it, still I had to set my teeth and carry out my superiors' instructions. As the man responsible for a district, these were all things there was no help for.

The two telegrams together were copied out and given over to Brother Zhang Zuoxing to pass on to Liu Shaokui and Liu Junqing. As for the elder Yu Qia and Zhao Zigang, the word was carried to them by mouth through Brother Shaokui; and Jiang Futian of the French police was notified of it by Group Leader Bi of "New Group One." In its first stage the affair went only so far as this, and in fact no action was taken; those notified, too, made no particular response. By rights the "Shanghai District" might well have taken the lead and called a "talk-meeting" or a "preparatory meeting"; but because it was inconvenient for all to gather, I did not set about it in earnest either. It cannot be gainsaid that I had a mind of my own: in the end I held that it would not yield the looked-for effect.

Then again, on the "Shanghai District's" side: if this affair were to be managed, a portion of manpower must be thrown into it, yet the several assistant secretaries we had were already pressed breathless by their heavy business, and, what is more, none of them had a bent for this kind of work; even to send one man to take part, I could truly pick out no one. After much hard thought, I hit at last upon a man—only, where he now might be, I still had no notion.

This man was our schoolfellow Qi Nanpu, who had taken his secret-service training with us at the Hong Ancestral Hall in Nanjing. In the winter of the twenty-first year, Qi Nanpu, Yang Ying, and I, we three, were sent to Beiping to set up work; and from that time on he had made the gathering of social intelligence his chief task, taking part in the doings of the secret societies. He was a "socialized" figure, easy in his manner of living to draw near to the common folk at the base; to ask him to take charge of this part of the work would be far better than to leave it to me. So I telegraphed Mr. Dai, set out my reasons, and asked that our schoolfellow Qi Nanpu be transferred to Shanghai to take charge of this work. Mr. Dai agreed; and before long Brother Qi Nanpu, too, arrived in Shanghai.

My way of doing it was to pipe softly and drum lightly, to keep a low posture: I did not mean to work up any large-scale "workers' movement," nor did I plan to form an empty, hollow "Workers'-Movement Committee." I asked only that, kept within the bounds of intelligence work, I might set among the mass of workers a few working lines of some use, and, at need, drive down into the base of society for occupational cover—that would do. If it should indeed develop and come into its own, and gain a fair influence over the workers' movement, that would be a kind of windfall; in truth I dared not indulge so extravagant a hope.

Accordingly, the "Shanghai District" did no more than add, within the district headquarters itself, a "Labor-Movement Office," for which Brother Nanpu bore entire responsibility, and which stood in no lateral relation to any other department. To make communication with our superiors convenient, a cipher-clerk was transferred and attached to the "Labor-Movement Office," under Brother Nanpu's direction. On the field side, only "New Group One" set up a "labor-movement sub-group"; the other brigades and groups were left unchanged. My original thought was that everything should wait upon how Brother Nanpu's opening-up went, before any further decision.

The "Labor-Movement Office" that Brother Qi Nanpu directed was set up in an apartment house on Ladu Road in the French Concession; he had come with his household, so there was no need to find other cover—thus he settled in. After this, all was laid to his charge, and I made contact with him but now and again; he, for his part, was pressing forward there, groping his way with great zeal.

Because the scale was small, the "Shanghai District" drew up no separate budget, but merely added a little to the office expenses, and that served. Liu Shaokui and Liu Junqing never once offered an opinion; nor did Jiang Futian. Strangest of all, Mr. Dai never again asked after the matter. Things being so, there was nothing amiss in my way of doing it. And Brother Nanpu, because of this stretch of experience, was after the victory in the War of Resistance engaged as a mainstay of a government-registered people's body, the "Committee for Social Enterprises ————," and posted as the man responsible for the Tianjin side. This committee was managed by Messrs. Xu Liang and Xu Weibin, founding cadres of the "Juntong Bureau"; its full name was very long, and I can no longer recall it clearly.

Nor was the labor-movement organization without its achievements. According to the material furnished by Brother Bi Gaokui, leader of "New Group One," there is a passage that runs thus: "The workers of Shanghai stand first in number in the whole country; the workers who took part in the Northern Expedition and in the War of Resistance all showed courage and made their sacrifices—this was a force not to be slighted. When Comrade Qi Nanpu was ordered to Shanghai to push the labor-movement work, 'New Group One' thereupon set up a 'labor-movement sub-group.' Besides the leader, held by myself, its members were He Zhicheng, Bei Bu, Zhang Can, Xu Meiping, Liu Yunsheng, Yin Wenfa, You Shaoxi, and others, spread through such transport and industrial units as the tramcar company, the ——xin cotton mill, the waterworks company, and the railway engineering section. Their more concrete showing, weighted toward our side of the work, was this: tram conductors carried arms and ammunition for us; factory workers kept demolition stores for us, and helped in the work of sabotage, and the like. It is a pity that after the 'Shanghai District' suffered one great reverse the thing was, unhappily, broken off midway; else its prospect of development could truly not have been measured."

Weighing again the practice and the argument of Brother Bi Gaokui quoted above, it may be that the attitude and view I had earlier held toward labor-movement work were somewhat off the mark, for they were a little too passive.

Writing to this point draws out not only a thread of memory but stirs, too, some feeling. In those days the workmen taken on to join the labor-movement work were, every one, volunteers; only when carrying out a task were they given, as circumstances allowed, a little activity-money. Yet in our inner personnel-marks they were listed as "employed persons"—that is, unofficial workers, or probationers under observation. Of these, some had been reported up and put on record; some still rested only in the "Shanghai District's" personnel-marks. (What is here called "personnel-marks" was no register; it may have been some set of signs or ciphers, which only the man in charge could tell apart.) On ordinary days it came to nothing; but once some mishap befell—the work failing, an identity laid bare, capture and sacrifice, or the loss of goods and money and the like—then troubles multiplied. And the aftermath? Our own responsible departments would each hold to its own word and shove off the blame, yet still could not settle the real problem; while the very persons who bore the harm or suffered the pain—those men of resolve and those martyrs whom we had "employed"—all became, through and through, "nameless heroes." Cases of this kind, to speak of the labor side alone, befell both among the men Brother Nanpu had developed directly and within the "labor-movement sub-group" that Brother Gaokui headed; and not once or twice only.

Besides, cases of "employed persons" giving their lives for the work, and for the War of Resistance too, were many more. According to Brother Shi Hecheng—a member of Bi Gaokui's "New Group One," who once served in the police and is now retired—who this year (the seventy-second) wrote from America in June and spoke of things past, he recalls that after he was posted to Shanghai in the twenty-ninth year, he developed, on his own account, and took on two "employed persons" to join the action work: one was Zhang Xingqiu, one was Zhu Tieying. Though Brother Hecheng's letter did not say whether these were true names or aliases, after forty years and more he still remembered them so clearly that they may well have been the men's own names. Once, leading Zhang and Zhu, he set out to raid the puppet Reserve Bank by way of warning; and unhappily, the two men Zhang Xingqiu and Zhu Tieying gave their lives for the country in this very action. Brother Hecheng's letter wrote: "Recalling my alias of those days, it was Bao Yueren, and afterward I used Peng Jun again. As for the employed persons, the two martyrs Zhang Xingqiu and Zhu Tieying, they gave their lives for the country in the affair of the puppet Reserve Bank."

Of the raid on the puppet Reserve Bank, action was taken twice in all, and of it I still keep some faint impression; but as for the two martyrs Zhang and Zhu giving their lives for the country, not I alone but even their group leader, Brother Bi Gaokui, could no longer remember them—truly we have failed the dead; a sin, a sin! As to how Zhang and Zhu came to grief and even to sacrifice, I have wholly lost all recollection; making a supposition from the circumstances of the time, it is very likely they were seized on the spot by men of the police station and then handed over to the Shanghai Japanese gendarmerie, and, because the Reserve Bank was newly set up by the Wang puppets, were again delivered by the Japanese gendarmerie to the puppet "Special Operations Headquarters," and were at the last put to death by them. Whether it was so, I shall take a chance to ask Brother Shi Hecheng again; what he knows must be far more detailed than what he wrote in his letter.

Since the two martyrs Zhang Xingqiu and Zhu Tieying were "employed persons" in their lifetimes, whether they were ever reported up and set on record is truly hard to say; and if there was no record, then in the Bureau's "annals" the two of them very likely have no "name and register" at all. If that be so, the more ought I here to pay my respectful homage to the two martyrs Zhang Xingqiu and Zhu Tieying, and with reverent pen set down a record of them.
Below I excerpt once more a passage of recollection from Brother Shi Hecheng's letter to Brother Huang Zhiyuan:

"As for the working instances I can still remember—on the ninth of the eleventh month of the twenty-eighth year of the Republic, my superiors handed me a two-inch black-and-white photograph, in which three men stood side by side; the one in the middle was named as the target, and on the eleventh of the same month, toward evening, before a certain grand hotel on Avenue Edward VII, he was dealt with. When I saw the paper the next morning, I learned for the first time that it was Shao Fanjiu." According to another source, it was on the thirteenth of the eleventh month, at the Xixing Inn on East Zilaihuo Street in the French Concession.

Again, according to what the Chongqing Ta Kung Pao carried: "Central News Agency, Hong Kong, telegram of the fourteenth, Shanghai dispatch: at eight o'clock on the night of the thirteenth, on Avenue Edward VII an assassination occurred. The dead man was named Shao Fanjiu, upward of thirty years of age, who served as an assistant in the office of the lawyer Chen Huapeng and also worked in a bureau of the traitor Wang in western Shanghai. About seven o'clock on the night of the thirteenth, at a friend's bidding he dined at the Old Canton Restaurant on Avenue Edward VII; afterward, walking with four fellow-diners as far as East Zilaihuo Street, a quarrel of words arose among them, and one of them at once drew a pistol and fired at Shao, four shots in all, every one striking Shao in a vital spot, so that he fell to the ground and died on the instant. The post constable hurried up and took one of the party into custody, carrying him to the station for questioning."

In the time, the place, and the particulars of these three accounts there are discrepancies; yet even so this must be reckoned the nearest to the truth. I privately hold that the historical records all men acknowledge are, for the most part, likewise.

As I understand it, Shao Fanjiu was a cousin's nephew of Shao Lizi, and also the brother-in-law of a certain high cadre of our Bureau; he had trained in one of the Bureau's training classes and was a member of the body; because he turned his coat and went over to the puppets, the order came to sanction him. Whether there was yet some other circumstance behind it, since it was a charge given from above, cannot be known.

Brother Shi Hecheng wrote again in his letter: "Next was, in the early summer of the twenty-ninth year, on Yuyuan Road, the affair of Chen ——, dealt with by me, with Liu —— and Xia Yanfu to help; after your brother had struggled free of two White Russian bodyguards, I was lucky to get safely away from the scene, and when I got back to the Dazhong Hospital, Niangniang said: 'Mr. Shi, that face of yours is like a dead man's.' But this time we lost two 'fellows.'"

In this case I truly cannot recall who Chen —— was, nor can I find it in any source. Liu —— and Xia Yanfu were both members of "New Group One." The Dazhong Hospital, set up on Avenue Edward VII, was the resting-place of Brother Huang Zhiyuan and Brother Shi Hecheng; "Niangniang" means an aunt—a Shanghai term of respect for an elder or a peer among women. And the "Niangniang" here spoken of was none other than the own younger sister of Brother Huang Zhiyuan's wife, and the Dazhong Hospital was hers to run. In truth, at that time Brother Hecheng's wife, Brother Zhiyuan's wife, and her younger sister were all giving their aid to our work, or serving as cover, without pay. Though they were not our workers, yet, stirred by patriotic feeling and by the bond of kin, they braved danger and hardship just the same, helping in it without a backward look. So it must be said that they, too, were nameless heroes—and more remarkable, more to be revered. The most telling line in Brother Hecheng's letter lies in that "that face of yours is like a dead man's": one may well imagine how a man who had just finished a sanction and grappled with two White Russian bodyguards, and was lucky to break free and come back, could have any good color in his face; I hold this truer, and of more meaning, than any describing of a man's valor. "We lost two 'fellows'" means that in the safe withdrawal and the struggle with the foe they lost two pistols in all.

There were a few more lines in the letter: "Next again, in the early winter of the twenty-ninth year, was the affair of Luda on Route Frelupt; and after that the affair of Duge on Route Say Zoong. When you, elder brother (meaning Brother Huang Zhiyuan), and I had finished, we sat in a French Concession omnibus and were all but run down by two French constables—a near thing! To this day, thinking of it, it is still as though it were yesterday."

What manner of man Luda was, and what sort of case it was, I can no longer remember, nor for the moment can I find any material bearing on it; though I have found that on the fifteenth of the eleventh month of the twenty-ninth year a certain Luding was sanctioned, yet "da" and "ding" differ by a single character, and, to avoid putting the wrong cap on the wrong head, I can here only hold the matter in reserve for now.

"Duge" is a transliteration; he was a Frenchman, holding the post of superintendent of police administration in the French Concession's Municipal Council, of no small standing. Because he aided the Japanese and made himself our enemy, he was sanctioned. The time was the seventeenth of the twelfth month of the twenty-ninth year, the place before No. 24 on Route Père Bassett in the French Concession. This, again, differs from the Route Say Zoong that Brother Shi Hecheng named in his letter—perhaps because the road-names are near in sound. This case Brother Hecheng carried out in person, and he was the more thoroughly familiar with the streets of Shanghai; his account, it would seem, should be taken as the reliable one.

The closing line of Brother Shi Hecheng's letter to Brother Huang Zhiyuan was: "The past is mist and cloud; it is truly hard to call it all back at once." And so this story, too, we here bring to a stop.

Touching the valiant sacrifices of "New Group One," Brother Liu Yuanshen once brought up a thing grievous to hear, whose gist ran thus. Comrade Tao Lianfang, a member of "New Group One" (a schoolfellow of the Guizhou training class), was, after his capture in an action, shut up in "No. 76"; through examination and the ordeal of torture, he came through that time of suffering after all. Some while later, in a half-freed state, he was forced off to Huzhou (Wuxing, in Zhejiang) to gather intelligence for them. Comrade Tao Lianfang seized this chance to make contact with our Bureau once more—what we called, in our term, "re-linking." But unlooked-for, this was found out by Wang Lubin, head of the "Huzhou Station" under the puppet "Special Operations Headquarters." This Wang Lubin stood in a special relation to Wan Lilang: his younger sister Wang Min had been a typist, whom Wan Lilang took as a concubine, so that he enjoyed no little of Wan's trust, and in all his dealings and toward all men he was utterly a scoundrel, and overbearing besides. Whether it was his own notion or done at Wan's bidding is not known, but he actually joined with the local Japanese gendarmerie and, taking the cover of night, had Comrade Tao Lianfang bound up and buried alive—so that the living saw him no more, and of the dead there was left no corpse!
This is the plainest, most certain of facts, and one more instance of our comrades—hundreds upon thousands of them—dying in the work behind enemy lines.

As the back-office comrades sat together in loose talk, one comrade proposed to me that, if circumstances allowed, it would do no harm to make a general inspection of the field units, so as to learn the actual state of the work in each, to open a channel between high and low, inner and outer, and at the same time to give the comrades in charge of each unit a word of comfort and cheer. This was indeed a good notion, and by word of mouth I accepted it; yet in my heart I had another thought. I held that in our "Shanghai District" the channels between high and low, inner and outer, ran clear and unblocked—an opinion could be voiced anytime, anywhere, with no need to open a channel afresh. And the state of a field unit's work was not a thing to be wholly grasped by meeting its head once and exchanging a few words; that would be but empty form. As for the notion that a single inspection could work encouragement, that too was doubtful; and besides, I had no such great influence. So, provided one held the functioning of the organization in hand, all else was secondary.

For the present, what I meant to do was still, true to my first intent, to take up contact at the key points. In the early part of the twenty-ninth year, to expand the ordering of the action brigades, I had several talks with my schoolfellow Jiang Anhua, commander of the "Third Action Brigade."

My first impression of my schoolfellow Anhua was this: that a man from elsewhere should be able to keep his footing on the Shanghai Bund was already no small thing. That his abilities were strong goes without saying; what made him most to be trusted was that spirit of his—self-starting, self-moving, brave and never at rest in the work. If one must find out his weak point, it would be that, having no historical roots in the old structure of society, he could not yet break into the core of the local powers, so that in the disposition of the work there remained the regret of a reach not deep enough. To put it plainer: inside lines laid against such targets as the puppet Shanghai mayor Fu Xiao'an, or Zhang Xiaolin, that evil power who supplied the enemy, could never find a reliable thread or connection.

What I meant to discuss with Jiang Anhua, commander of the Third Brigade, was one theme and two methods. The theme was the strengthening of the action force. Method one: I hoped that his brigade, on the principle of not enlarging its establishment, would build up its strength, and best of all that every detachment should have the power to act on its own; among the present men, any not fit for this kind of work might be recalled to the rear for training or posted elsewhere—weeding out the weak and keeping the strong, that is—their vacancies to be filled by taking on men on the spot. Method two: to talk over with Commander Jiang whether he could recommend a fit candidate to form up a separate action brigade besides, so that at need it might act jointly with his brigade, and even that the two might support one another. To the first he agreed to put in a written report; as to the second, he said he must think it over with care—whether there was a fit man equal to the charge, he could not for the moment name.

Every time I met with Jiang Anhua, the contact was made beforehand through Miss Xiao Jieying's "liaison station," and the place of meeting was that "liaison station" itself. As mentioned before, the "Shanghai District" kept many "courier stations" and "liaison stations"; this one that Miss Xiao Jieying directed was but one among them. Its task, besides keeping contact with the "Third Action Brigade," was to hold a fixed link with the "Loyal and Patriotic Army" as well. There is, as it happens, a history behind this: the "liaison station" took the Xiao house for its cover—or rather, it was set up in the Xiao house. When Zhou Weilong (Daosan), the former Chief of the "Shanghai District," held concurrently the post of director of the "Loyal and Patriotic Army Office," the Xiao house was the "Loyal Army's" place of liaison, and so had connection with all its chief men. After the writer took over as Chief of the "Shanghai District," he too, seizing the convenience, kept up through it a half-official, half-private relation with the "Loyal Army." And after Brother Daosan took over as commander-in-chief of the "Loyal Army," this relation grew the closer. For Brother Daosan and I had trained in the same class at the Central Training Corps in Chongqing, and got on well together, and had given each other our word that we would keep in touch and seek to work together in our undertakings. As for what tricks he got up to after the victory in the War of Resistance, down to the fatal end he brought upon himself, of that I know nothing at all. This is all true talk, and idle talk too; it may as well be left unsaid.
Speaking of the Xiao house, there is truly much worth telling, and "Nameless Heroes" ought to set down a record of it.

The head of the Xiao house, the venerable Mr. Xiao Huanwen, was a man of Hunan; before the War of Resistance he had worked in the Shanghai Municipal Police Bureau, and after it broke out, when Zhou Weilong was director of the "Loyal Army's Shanghai Office," he took charge of the liaison with the "Loyal Army." The venerable Mr. Xiao Huanwen had three daughters and two sons, all of them bound up with the work of the "Juntong Bureau."

The eldest daughter, Xiao Shuying, whom all called Elder Sister Xiao. Her husband, Chen Zhiju, was a man of Xiangxiang in Hunan (some say of Hang County in Zhejiang), a graduate of the second regular class of the Zhejiang Police Officers' School, who had served as an inspector at the Shanghai Post-and-Telegraph Censorship Office. When the War of Resistance against Japan first broke out, Chief Zhou Weilong transferred Chen Zhiju to be leader of the "Dachang-District Field Work Group" of Shanghai; and not long after the fighting began, Chen was, unhappily, blown to death on the field by an enemy plane, not a bone of him left—the first of the two houses of Xiao and Chen to fall in the work. At Chen's death he left two sons, both of tender years; Elder Sister Xiao not only reared the orphans to grown men but carried on Chen's unfinished will, serving the body still. Elder Sister Xiao's elder son, Chen Zhaokui, once served as head of the Datong sub-bureau of the Taipei City Police, and was promoted besides to be director of the Taipei City Vehicle-Supervision Office; he is now a counselor of the Taiwan Provincial Government. The younger son has done well too in trade—so Heaven has eyes after all.

The second daughter, whose name I do not know, though she took no formal part in our work, yet we used more than once the rice shop her husband's family kept in Nanshi, Shanghai, as cover for the work. During that time, because the "Shanghai District" itself met with mishap again and again, Second Sister Xiao's husband's family was, to some degree, dragged in and implicated. In a case where there was neither office to hold nor pay to draw, this was truly rare; and never once did they utter a word of complaint.

The third daughter, Xiao Jieying, was the youngest, and all called her Third Sister. She it was who headed one of the "liaison stations" belonging to the "Shanghai District," and had once directed the "inner courier station" besides. In those days Third Miss Xiao was still an unwed maid at home, living with her old father and her eldest sister, so that the home was the "station" and the "station" was the home. Third Sister was clever beyond the common, and had no little daring, and was skilled above all at meeting each turn as it came. For the "Shanghai District" she coped, first and last, with many a sudden turn, and on her it depended that danger was turned to safety—an able cadre indeed. From the end of the thirtieth year of the Republic to the beginning of the thirty-first, the writer, together with Xiao Jieying, Jiang Anhua, and several others, went through a spell of trouble whose course was tangled enough that a few words could hardly make it plain; I must leave it for the fourth volume of "Nameless Heroes."
The above records the three sisters of the Xiao house and Elder Sister Xiao's husband Chen Zhiju; below I record the Xiao brothers.

Xiao Fuquan, a graduate of Kwang Hua University in Shanghai, had served as secretary of the "Loyal Army's" Shanghai Office, and was afterward transferred to be a directly-attached courier of the "Shanghai District." I met him several times at the Xiao house, but never talked with him deeply. After the victory in the War of Resistance he served as a section head in the inspectorate of the Songhu Garrison Headquarters; after coming to Taiwan he held office in the police, and for years was chief of the police bureau in one outlying county after another; I hear he still serves in the Taiwan Provincial Government, though we have not met these many years.

Xiao Zhangquan was the youngest brother of the Xiao house. In Mr. Zheng Xiuyuan's notes he is set down as commander of the Seventh Action Brigade of the "Shanghai District"; but to my memory it should rightly be the Eighth Brigade. Was it not mentioned before that I asked my schoolfellow Jiang Anhua to recommend a man, meaning to enlarge the action establishment and form up one more brigade? Afterward, he proposed to me the raising-up of Xiao Zhangquan. Why do I say "raising-up"? Because Zhangquan was too young in years, and short of standing; yet he was brave beyond the common and daring beyond his fellows. I held that to have these qualities was already hard to come by, so I reported it up, asked that he be made commander, and it was granted.

Xiao Zhangquan was at that time no more than twenty-four or twenty-five, unwed, with a strong political sense, free of the bad habits of the common city youth, pure and true and altogether lovable. Because he was young, what he lacked was a little seasoning. The forming of the "Eighth Action Brigade of the Shanghai District" owed not a little to Jiang Anhua's help; and my schoolfellow Jiang gave Xiao Zhangquan, too, much earnest instruction.

The chief task I laid on the Eighth Brigade was the work of sabotage on the several railway lines around the outskirts of the Shanghai region, and above all along the Nanjing–Shanghai line. The thought behind it was that in the Shanghai city proper and the two Concessions there were already the forces of several action brigades, enough to answer the need; in fact it was much wanted that the disposition be more dispersed, to widen the effect of the work.

It was in the course of the twenty-ninth year that the "Shanghai District" ordered the Eighth Brigade to send a man to reconnoiter first the stretch from Shanghai to Suzhou, the aim being to survey the targets of sabotage anew. Little did any know that Zhangquan, offering himself of his own will, went alone, a single man with a single gun. It was learned afterward that he had first taken the train to Suzhou and then walked back; but at what spot the mishap befell him none could tell—word of him was utterly cut off, he went and did not return. After a long while, more than half a year in all, it was confirmed that he had died a cruel death at the hands of the Suzhou Japanese gendarmerie. Judging by the martyr Xiao Zhangquan's character, and by his faithful keeping of his charge, it is very likely that, holding fast and telling nothing, he was tortured to the utmost and gave his life for righteousness; his heroism may well be imagined.

The above is the Xiao family's household loyalty—the venerable Mr. Xiao Huanwen and his two sons, three daughters, and one son-in-law, and the misfortunes they suffered for our work; and the most piteous of all is that the eldest son-in-law Chen Zhiju and the youngest son Xiao Zhangquan both fell so utterly that not even their bodies remained!

The mention above of the "Loyal and Patriotic Army" cannot but call to mind the case, on the Christmas Eve of the twenty-eighth year, in which the three men of resolve Ma Hetu, Yue Qingjiang, and Ding Baoling valiantly sanctioned Chen Dirong (Mingchu). In that case, unlooked for, they also, along with him, struck down grievously wounded He Xingjian (Tianfeng)—who had deserted the "Loyal Army" and gone over to the puppets, and had once been commander of the "Second Column of the Loyal and Patriotic Army" and commander of the "Songhu Headquarters of the Loyal and Patriotic Army"—so that, taken to hospital, he died past all cure.

In the third chapter above, the telling leaned only on Chen Mingchu, and touching He Xingjian a strange episode much worth recording was let slip—an episode that holds hidden within it, moreover, many a secret from which one may well take warning; so I set it down here by way of supplement.

Between the latter half of the twenty-seventh year and the first half of the twenty-eighth, troubles sprang up thick within the "Loyal and Patriotic Army," and its organization was less than sound; of which the outline may be seen in two telegrams of Mr. Dai Yunong—one to Zhou Weilong, director of the "Loyal Army's Shanghai Office," and one to Yu Zuobai, its deputy commander-in-chief.
First, Mr. Dai's telegram to Zhou Weilong:

"To my honored Brother Renzhong (Zhou's assumed name): Your brother has just reached Changsha from Hankou, and makes ready to set out tomorrow for Nanchang; at the latest by the twelfth I shall reach Tunxi. This journey is wholly to settle all that touches the Loyal and Patriotic Army. It is my thought to summon the responsible delegates sent by the several detachments along the Pudong and Nanjing–Shanghai lines, to come by way of Ningbo to Jinhua and confer face to face on all things; best of all, let the office also send a man who knows the true state of the several units to come along. I beg you to wire your reply to Changsha at once, that word may be passed on. Your brother, Miao, respectfully."
Second, Mr. Dai's telegram to Yu Zuobai:

"Jinhua, to be passed at once to my honored Brother Zuobai: Have the delegates of the Nanjing–Shanghai detachments reached Jinhua yet? I think of it much! Of late the special commissioners sent from Shanghai to the several detachments have for the most part been unable to work in true good faith with the men in charge of them, and there is much mutual suspicion, even to the point of stirring up incidents; this comes, to be sure, of the poor ability of the men I sent, or of some selfish, self-seeking design and want of a sense of the whole. Yet that the men in charge of the several detachments should scheme to hold troops for their own safety, or, under the name of saving the country, to plot their own rise in rank and gain, and the pushing-out of those not of their party—of all these turns of mind it is truly hard to be rid. So I beg you, brother, to admonish the delegates in every way, and to make earnest explanation, that there may be improvement hereafter, and no shame brought upon the Loyal and Patriotic Army. As for the misconduct of the several commissioners, your brother has already wired Renzhong (Zhou Weilong) to correct it sternly. Your brother, Li, respectfully."

In these two telegrams the sense is plain enough, and needs no explaining. To show the general state of the "Loyal Army" in those days, they are enough. Below I set down again He Xingjian's standing and place within the "Loyal Army," which makes it the easier to see how things lay. At that time Mr. Dai's hopes of He Xingjian were high, and he leaned on him the more heavily; this is clear at a glance in Dai's telegram to He, whose content ran as follows:

"To my honored Brother Xingjian: Your brother came from Chongqing into Shaanxi on the sixth, and shall stay here about a week more. Just now a telegram forwarded from Chongqing brings the glad news that your banners have reached the shores of Shanghai—a great comfort! In this late upheaval at Shanghai, all our work there has taken a grievous blow; and tracing the chief cause, in matters inner and outer, high and low, the whole fault gathers upon the one person of Brother Daosan. Therefore, for the command and setting-in-order of the Loyal and Patriotic Army hereafter, I am resolved to ask you, brother, under the title of resident commander at Shanghai, to set up a Songhu Headquarters and there to plan and command. Your brother has already transferred Brother Xu —— to be senior staff officer of the headquarters, and Brother —— must surely have reached Shanghai by now. I beg you, brother, to organize at once a simple but tight headquarters; for all its personnel, the standard may be those among the former Shanghai Office's men who can keep a footing in Shanghai and can travel the Nanjing–Shanghai line; any already exposed in Shanghai should be transferred at once to work at the Tunxi head office, or given funds and dismissed. Brother! The success or failure of the Loyal and Patriotic Army is the success or failure of our whole undertaking. You, brother, are a founding hero of this army; in going to Shanghai now you shoulder a heavy charge, and I beg you to spur on in every way the responsible comrades, to stand ever on the ground of the Three Principles of the People, to save the nation and save the people, to hold to the Leader's intent, to resist the enemy with resolve and cherish the people; and toward those men the former Shanghai Office sent to the several detachments, if any know not self-respect nor have a sense of the whole, they should be looked into and dealt with at once, and there must not be the least scruple or indulgence. Your brother, Ling, respectfully."

Not long after this, He Xingjian turned traitor and went over to the puppets, and took besides the title the Wang puppets gave him of "Commander of the Second Route of the Anti-Communist National-Salvation Army," and so, brazen-faced, served the enemy.

The puppet forces made "anti-Communism" their banner, and yet He Xingjian was in secret in league with the Communist Party; were this said on bare word alone, it might be hard to bring men to believe. As luck would have it, the other day the writer came upon a pamphlet: in the so-called "revolutionary historical materials" published in February of 1981 (the seventieth year of the Republic) by the Chinese Communists' "Literary and Historical Materials Publishing House," there is, in a piece titled "In the Heart of the Enemy" by Zhang Zhiyi—now deputy head of the Chinese Communists' Central United Front Work Department, who in those days had likewise done "united-front" work under the "Jiangsu Provincial Committee"—a passage of self-confession, whose content ran, in the original, as follows:

"The Provincial Committee (the writer's note: meaning the Chinese Communists' 'Jiangsu Provincial Committee') set up in addition a Military Committee, to open up military activity in the Shanghai region, with Comrade Zhang Aiping (the writer's note: now defense minister of the puppet Chinese Communist regime) as its secretary, and Yu Lijin, Chen Jiakang, and myself (the writer's note: Zhang Zhiyi refers to himself) as members. With the Military Committee's consent, I, through my connection with Xiang Songpo (styled Haiqian), then a Hong Gang chief of much renown in Shanghai, carried on activity on the military side, and got hold of a title—the Third Brigade of the First Detachment, commissioned by the Guerrilla General Headquarters of the Jiangsu-Zhejiang Action Committee of the National Government's Military Affairs Commission. The commander of the First Detachment, He Xingjian (styled Tianfeng), was an old soldier and a Hong Gang man; at that time, because he wished to win the trust of our side, so that he might go on to win the trust of Xiang Haiqian, he professed himself willing to heed our word. (I was a man of the Chinese Communist side, and He knew it. He later became Dai Li's man, then presently surrendered to the Japanese and to Wang, and was shot dead by men Dai Li sent, in the French Concession.) At that time He commissioned me to be captain-secretary of that detachment headquarters, and Comrade Yu Jiyi (then named Yu Hua) to be lieutenant-secretary; both left early on account of illness. Then, with the organization's leave, I formed the Third Brigade under the Hong Gang name, and roused the youth of the several salvation bodies and refugee shelters to join this guerrilla band—some five hundred and more in number—and drew two hundred and fifty long and short guns each, with four hand grenades issued to every man besides. The Guerrilla General Headquarters (the writer's note: meaning the 'Loyal and Patriotic Army') sent a graduate of the fourth Whampoa class to be lieutenant-colonel and brigade commander (we did not let him get real power), and our Party member Wang Jiguang (Ren Tiefeng) was major and deputy brigade commander. The company, sector, and platoon leaders were all filled by secret Party members or progressive elements; but a pity it is that the leader's work was not effective, and, with the wrecking of the reactionaries added to it, before long Wang Jiguang, on his own authority, took a dozen or more cadres and fled into hiding, so that the work came to failure. Afterward Wang Jiguang ran off to Nanjing, and our Party's delegation resident there expelled him from the Party on the charge of flight."

This memoir-like thing above, written by Zhang Zhiyi, (present) deputy head of the Chinese Communists' Central United Front Work Department—judging it by the writer's own long experience in handling intelligence materials—though a part of it is to be believed, is yet not free of tangled errors and shameless bragging. I here point out, in the order of its own words, its several points of true and false, of real and empty, of concealment and exaggeration, as follows.

Zhang Zhiyi writes: "I, through my connection with Xiang Songpo, then a Hong Gang chief of much renown in Shanghai …" and so on and so forth. Mark those two words, "through": they carry a great deal of borrowing another's name, of passing off a false thing, of covering the sky to cross the sea—this too is a Communist's constant device. To get at the truth: did he borrow Xiang Songpo's name? or had he already got his consent? All this is glossed over with those two words, "through." Then the text goes on: "carried on activity on the military side, and got hold of … a title." A "title," so called, ought to have a set procedure of issue; to say it was "got hold of" is plainly out of the normal course. What is telling is that in these few sentences he lets the fox's tail show without knowing it. How so? The "Loyal and Patriotic Army," belonging to the "Jiangsu-Zhejiang Action Committee," was a body of the people's armed force resisting Japan; the Communist Party did not resist Japan, but busied itself solely with worming into the ranks of the resisters to play its tricks—and yet dressed it up with the fine name of "carrying on military activity." A wolf's whelp's ambition it is, in very truth, and detestable in the extreme.

Zhang's text goes on: "The commander of the First Detachment, He Xingjian, was an old soldier and a Hong Gang man; at that time, because he wished to win the trust of our side so that he might go on to win the trust of Xiang Haiqian, he professed himself willing to heed our word." But think: He Xingjian was a Hong Gang man, and Xiang Songpo was a Hong Gang man too—did he need first to win the Communists' trust before he could go on to win Xiang Songpo's? This is a string of ghost-talk from end to end—puffing himself up.

Zhang writes: "He later became Dai Li's man, then presently surrendered to the Japanese and to Wang, and was shot dead by men Dai Li sent, in the French Concession." In truth, He Xingjian was from the first a worker under Mr. Dai, and only later fell into league with the Communists—here is one more plain proof of his turning right and wrong upside down. As for whose man was whose, the feudal cast of mind is still not shaken off. Only the one sentence, "shot dead by men Dai Li sent," may be counted true. Yet the place was at the far end of Yuyuan Road, an extra-Settlement road of the International Settlement, and not the French Concession; in this, again, he has it wrong.

Look again at the Communists' devices: this crew of Zhang Zhiyi's, borrowing the name of salvation, roused the patriotic youth, formed a guerrilla band of five hundred and more, and drew arms from the Loyal Army head office; yet when the head office sent a brigade commander, they would not let him get real power—proof enough that their hearts already harbored ill from the start.

And when at last they met with failure, they laid the blame falsely on the "wrecking of the reactionaries"—one mouth, two flaps of skin indeed, turning it this way and that and slandering as they please.

In these few hundred words of narrative alone there are so many faults, and some small points not even reckoned in; whence one may know that in reading the Communists' stuff one cannot but be careful—one lapse of attention, and they have you "wound" up.

From the "Loyal Army" I have come to He Xingjian, and from He Xingjian to the Communist Party; and though it strays somewhat far afield, it too springs from feeling, and means only to point out the base doings of the Communists. The main thing is still to show that the "Juntong Bureau" of that day marked only He Xingjian's turning traitor to the puppets, and never found out that he was already in secret league with the Communists. Yet in the telegram Mr. Dai sent He Xingjian there are a few lines that give one pause. Mr. Dai's message says: "You, brother, are a founding hero of this army; in going to Shanghai now you shoulder a heavy charge, and I beg you to spur on in every way the responsible comrades, to stand ever on the ground of the Three Principles of the People, to save the nation and save the people, to hold to the Leader's intent, to resist the enemy with resolve and cherish the people." That one sentence above all—"to stand ever on the ground of the Three Principles of the People, to save the nation and save the people"—seems, whether toward the responsible cadres or toward He Xingjian himself, out of the common, a special hint; for Mr. Dai very, very seldom raised the question of "political standing" with his high subordinates in letter or telegram, and, having raised it here, could it be that he had caught some rumor on the wind? or had already grown wary of something?

There is yet another layer: whether He Xingjian's turning traitor to the puppets, and his constant mixing with the general run of men at "No. 76," was itself a snare laid by the Communists, in the hope of profiting thereby—this must be gone into a layer deeper.

Had it not been for the pointer given me by Mr. Xu Shouyan, and the precious materials he was good enough to bestow, in my poor "Nameless Heroes" one great matter would very nearly have been let slip.

This matter should be told from the beginning; and though in the order of the record it is somewhat out of sequence, there is no harm in going back once more to the end of the twenty-eighth year—the interval being short, the threads can still be joined, so that what goes before does not fail to meet what comes after.

In the third chapter above, the writer wrote only so far as the three righteous men, Ma Hetu and the rest, who on the Christmas Eve of the twenty-eighth year seized their chance and sanctioned Chen Dirong (Mingchu) and He Xingjian (Tianfeng), so bringing upon Mr. Wang Tianmu the great suffering of being dragged in; but more important than this, there were three good comrades of ours who lost their lives thereby, and became, of all things, the offerings in a "living sacrifice" at "No. 76"! Alas, the pity of it!

Mr. Xu Shouyan is an old comrade of the "Juntong Bureau," now in Taiwan, in the service of the Central Daily News. A month ago he wrote me a letter, of which I here excerpt the chief points as follows:

"My own elder brother Shouxin was formerly chief of the Guiyang head radio-station of our Bureau; by Mr. Dai's order he took over from Yang Zhenyi as chief communications inspector of the 'Shanghai District,' under the alias 'Zhu Chengwo.' Not long after taking up the post, on account of Chen Mingchu's defection, he was seized by 'No. 76' and shut up in one cell (within No. 76) with Xu Wenqi. Afterward, when Chen Mingchu was sanctioned, 'No. 76' turned its wrath upon my brother and, at five in the afternoon on the twenty-fifth of the twelfth month of the twenty-eighth year, brought him out and shot him (the executioners were Wan Lilang and Lin Zhijiang). Even as he went to his death he cried out again and again, 'Long live the Republic of China!' 'Long live the Leader!'—and so, in heroism, gave his life for righteousness.

(Mr. Xu Shouyan's note: "Shouyan, by Mr. Dai's order, attended the 'April First Assembly' of the twenty-ninth year, and was received in audience by the Leader. At the head office of the Bureau I looked into the original files, and thereby came to learn the above.")

"Shouyan joined the body's work; from the twenty-fifth year onward he served as instructor and chief instructor of the fifth and sixth classes of the special-police course, and after the victory in the War of Resistance was transferred to be head of the Shanghai 'Post-and-Telegraph Censorship Office.' Later, at Nanjing, he met with Brother Xu Wenqi and was often in touch with him; and Brother Wenqi was good enough to spare the time to write, truthfully, the piece 'One of the Nameless Heroes Who Died in the Sino-Japanese War,' and to hand it to Shou—— for a keepsake. Though it has passed through the upheavals of war and flight, I never dared let it be lost, and have kept it safe to this day. I make bold to send a copy, and beg you to look it over.

"My elder brother Shouxin left one daughter, named Lihua, reared to womanhood by her grandmother, who has lived with Shouyan throughout; she now serves as a special commissioner of the Central Bank, is happily married, and her eldest daughter has already entered middle school. Mr. Zheng Xiuyuan took Lihua as a goddaughter, which may too be a comfort to my late brother in the world below. For forty years and more I have kept up an unbroken contact with Mr. Zheng Xiuyuan; of Shouyan's family affairs Mr. Xiuyuan knows in full detail, and a single inquiry will tell all."

The Mr. Yang Zhenyi mentioned in Mr. Xu Shouyan's letter was, when the "Shanghai District" met the "July Fourteenth Incident" in the twenty-eighth year, chief communications inspector for the Shanghai region; because his identity had been laid bare and he could no longer keep a footing in Shanghai, he was ordered elsewhere. The man who took over from Mr. Yang Zhenyi as chief inspector was Mr. Xu Shouxin (alias Zhu Chengwo). What needs explaining here is this: the chief communications inspector for the Shanghai region had a range of duty that covered the whole of Greater Shanghai; that is to say, apart from the "Shanghai District," which was one working unit fitted with a radio, every working unit in the Greater Shanghai region that had a radio came under his oversight. In working standing, the chief communications inspector was directly under the head office of the Bureau, on a level with the Chief of the "Shanghai District."

The capture of Mr. Xu Shouxin took place, in all likelihood, somewhere between the middle of the seventh month and the middle of the eighth month of the twenty-eighth year. The writer took up his post in the "Shanghai District" in the middle of the eighth month, and so has no way of knowing the course of Mr. Xu Shouxin's capture.

As for how the puppet "Special Operations Headquarters" (that is, "No. 76"), on the day after Chen Dirong (Mingchu) and He Xingjian (Tianfeng) were sanctioned, brought out from the cells the three comrades already seized—Zhou Xiliang, Xu Shouxin, and Yu Yanzhi—and put them to death, in a bloody revenge: what a bitter, what a maddening thing this is; by any reckoning the "Shanghai District" ought to have known of it, and yet it was let slip by me, and beyond blaming myself for my muddle-headedness I have truly nothing to say. Alone, I have shut my eyes and turned it over many times, and truly not a trace of it is left me. Now, thanks to Mr. Xu Shouyan's plain telling, that piece of history—the cruel sacrifice of two martyrs of ours—is saved from being buried; for which deep thanks are owed here.

Mr. Xu Shouyan mentions that the executioners who killed the martyr Xu Shouxin were the two men Wan Lilang and Lin Zhijiang; for want of other material to check it against, this can no longer be looked into. So far as the writer knows, Wan Lilang had at that moment but lately gone over to the puppets, and to curry favor and seek merit was only to be expected of him; that he should seize this chance to make his standing sure is not impossible. And sure enough, after Chen Mingchu was brought to justice, he succeeded to his vacant place and became chief of the First Section of the puppet "Special Operations Headquarters"—and this is the plainest, most certain of facts.

Speaking of Lin Zhijiang, I had known him since the twenty-second year of the Republic; in my impression he was a swaggering, strutting sort of man, who would of course do his share of disorderly things too. Yet later he turned his head after all and served the government, and was found out by the Japanese gendarmerie; and by the court-martial of the Japanese army's "Gun Unit" he was sentenced, on a charge of "communicating with the enemy," to ten years' imprisonment, held in the Ward Road Gaol in Shanghai, and let out only after the victory. Perhaps because his "conscience was ill at ease" and "his burden of guilt too heavy," he could not bring himself to face the world, and slipped away to Hong Kong to lie low from the storm. About the forty-first or forty-second year of the Republic, in poverty and ruin, he died of illness at Hong Kong.

At that time the men in power at "No. 76" were Ding Mocun and Li Shiqun, and those who decided to kill the two martyrs Xu Shouxin and Yu Yanzhi must surely have been the two traitors Ding and Li. Their arrogance was then at its height, lawless and heaven-defying; with no need to pass through any legal procedure, one proposing and the other chiming in, they could take a man's life at any moment. And before long these two, dog biting dog, came to open strife—and that too was all for the sake of one word: "power."

The piece "One of the Nameless Heroes Who Died in the Sino-Japanese War," written by Mr. Xu Wenqi and mentioned in Mr. Xu Shouyan's letter, is enough to describe the general scene before the martyr Xu Shouxin (Zhu Chengwo) gave his life for righteousness. Concerning this memorial work, the writer wrote to ask Mr. Xu Shouyan whether the piece had ever been published; he was good enough to reply as follows:

"The enclosure of Brother Wenqi's that I sent you last time was handed to Shouyan in person by Brother Wenqi when he was at the Nanjing office, with no copy kept back, and so it was never published abroad." The letter noted further: "In Biographical Literature (published in the eleventh month of the seventy-second year) there appears a work of Brother Wenqi's, telling how, during his term as warden of the Nanjing detention house, he kept guard over Chen Bijun and the other traitors; and within it there is mention of my brother's martyrdom, but only in passing, not published as a piece of its own."

This piece is an old work of Mr. Xu's from the thirtieth year; never published, and describing besides the great, fearless spirit of one who gave his life, I copy it out in full—and still there lingers the feeling that the words have not said all it meant.
Below is the full text; where explanation is needed, the writer appends notes of his own.

Zhu Chengwo—a native of Nanjing (the writer's added note: according to what Mr. Xu Shouyan told me by letter, his native place was Shitai County in Anhui Province), his true name was Xu Shouxin. I (the author, Mr. Xu Wenqi, refers to himself; and so below) came to know him at the house at No. 104 Aitang Road in Shanghai. He was the chief of a radio station, and held besides the post of the organization's radio-station overseer (the writer's added note: this means the "chief communications inspector for the Shanghai region of the Juntong Bureau"); I was secretary of the action head-brigade (the writer's added note: this "action head-brigade" belonged to the "Shanghai District," its commander Zhao Lijun, alias Ling Qiuyun). The offices of the action head-brigade were set up in another place; but because I had been assigned besides to compile military intelligence, I went every day to the headquarters. Chengwo said little on meeting a stranger, and I too held to silence on meeting a stranger, so that though in those days we saw each other almost daily, having no business to take us together, we went several months without ever once talking of anything side by side. Later Chen Mingchu defected, and we kept office in several places, so that apart from meeting at important conferences we saw each other still less. Not until the eighth month (of the twenty-eighth year), when he was seized, and the end of the tenth month, when I was seized, did we meet again—in a detention cell within No. 76 on Jessfield Road, Shanghai. At the first sight of me he said: "Who would have thought you would come here too—come in, sit down; come in and sit a while!" At that time we were shut in two rooms; I was assigned to the better-fitted one, and Chengwo's was the poorer. We lived next door to each other, and only each day could we meet and talk, and from time to time crack a joke together besides.

Chengwo was of an exceeding cleverness, but exceeding proud and stiff too; he wrote a fine hand, and was of a stately, handsome bearing, tall of body and fair of skin—one might well call him a beautiful man. After he was killed, not to speak of his fellow-sufferers, who grieved for him without end, even the men in the "Special Operations Headquarters" sighed over it, saying what a great pity it was—a man of such parts as he.

Before long he was moved into the room where I lived, and our time together grew the more, and we came the more to talk freely; he was not as hard to draw out as in the days when we had been colleagues—now there was nothing we did not speak of: the nation, society, the family, even the question of sex between man and woman, all came under our talk. In the same room there was besides a university professor, Dr. Wang Zhongqi, of a solemn, austere air on ordinary days, who before long joined in the talk too; he had been taken before me, and was skilled at telling fortunes, and in those days many asked him to tell theirs. Chengwo, having now nothing to do, went daily to learn fortune-telling from him; I, though by nature one who does not believe in fatalism, once asked him too, in those days, to reckon out a lifelong fortune for me.

Later we were all moved to the great gaol at the back, Chengwo still lodging with me in one room; and now we suffered indeed—eating, drinking, and the calls of nature, and sleep, all were awkward, and the room was so cramped, with eight men lodged together, that there was scarcely room even to turn about. At that time the wounds on my body (the writer's added note: got, I suppose, from the torture after capture) were not yet wholly healed, and, thrust into this little room where I could not stretch my sinews much, I felt it a bitterness beyond all. We had no time for walking either, and only by the excuse of relieving ourselves could we stir a little more upon the grass.

At that time Jiang Zhixiang, who had shared the front room, could already move about half-freely under watch and did not lodge with us; Dr. Wang Zhongqi too was given "favored treatment" and did not lodge in this little room. Those in the room were only Tang Yadong (the writer's added note: before his capture Comrade Tang was commander of the Third Action Brigade of the "Shanghai District"; see the "True Record of Three Perils on the Shanghai Shore" written by Mr. Zheng Xiuyuan), Xu Zhan (the writer's added note: before his capture Comrade Xu was deputy commander of the Third Action Brigade of the "Shanghai District"; see the same writing of Mr. Zheng Xiuyuan), Zhu Chengwo, and myself. Besides these, there were a few men I did not know.

Though Chengwo was then shut up with me, the men of No. 76 had already brought him out and talked with him, and it was said that in a few days his case would be settled, and they would give him some work to do besides. He was half in fear and half in gladness, his mind still unquiet: glad that he might move freely, in fear of how he could do work assigned by the enemy and the puppets.

In the long days when men are penned up with nothing to do, we would talk at large, and he told me many stories of his late wife who had died (the writer's added note: according to Mr. Xu Shouyan's letter: "My sister-in-law Zhu Cheng'e died first; when my brother came from Hong Kong to Shanghai he had already resolved to hold to the will of sacrifice for the country, and the alias 'Zhu Chengwo' was to keep her memory"). Husband and wife had been very tender in their love; she had been a schoolmate of his younger sister, and they had married for love, with the parents' consent, and had already borne a daughter (the writer's added note: according to Mr. Shouyan's letter: "My brother left one daughter, named Lihua, reared to womanhood by her grandmother, who has lived with Shouyan throughout; she now serves as a special commissioner of the Central Bank, is happily married, and her eldest daughter has already entered middle school. Mr. Zheng Xiuyuan took Lihua as a goddaughter, which may too be a comfort to my late brother in the world below"), whom I too had seen. For the love of his wife he had resolved to keep widowed three years before he would speak of marrying again; at that time his wife had been dead but a year and more, and he, unhappily, was again taken captive—truly one of the great regrets of this human world; and more unhappily still, whatever his wishes were, none of them could now be fulfilled.

He asked too after my family affairs and my marriage, and I told him frankly; at that time I kept always by me, never apart from me, a photograph of ——, and while I lodged in the gaol I had tucked it into an old book. One day he, sitting on my bed, caught sight of it, and, in all earnest and gravity, took the wrapping-paper of a packet of Ruby Queen cigarettes (the writer's added note: as I understand it, the cigarettes were brought in by the warders for a price; the "Ruby Queen" was a common cigarette, which northerners called "Fenbao" and Shanghai folk called the "Great Britain brand") and carefully wrapped that photograph up for me, saying besides: "How can you set another's photograph out so carelessly? This way it is easily soiled; let me wrap it up for you!" I watched him wrap it, and heard him speak, and my heart in that moment was moved beyond telling. In this the more may one mark how lofty was his character—truly worthy of reverence.

Of Chengwo's household I knew: before Chen Mingchu defected, in the days when I often went to the district office to work, we met from time to time. His father had died early, and his old mother yet lived; he had two younger brothers and two younger sisters, and a daughter of his own, who then lodged below-stairs at our district office as cover. His elder sister was already twenty-one or twenty-two, had left off her schooling, and had no work either. Later, only when Chen Mingchu defected, did she take up courier duty in the organization. The heavy burden of the living of Chengwo's whole household rested wholly on Chengwo's single supplying. Chengwo's death was not only a loss to the nation's organization—it was still more a loss to his whole family!

The heavens have their unforeseen storms, and man his fortune and misfortune of a morning or an evening; and the more so when we were then in such a setting as that—who could foretell life or death?! I remember that day was the twenty-fifth of the twelfth month, past eight in the morning, and still no gruel had been brought; ordinarily the gruel came at seven. Just as all were in doubt and guessing, we heard from the guards' talk that Chen Mingchu had been shot dead past three that night at the Wilden dance hall, so that within No. 76 all was in an uproar, men and horses overturned—so much so that they gave us no breakfast to eat either.

Before the Chen case befell, the Bureau had already planned to be rid of this traitor, and had sent men to kill him several times without success; and at the same time one Zhou Xiliang, who did counter-espionage work (the writer's added note: that is, a man who contrived to get into No. 76 as an inside line), was again found out. At that time I saw him in the gaol, and it was said that he had borne severe torture to the full, yet in the end never gave up a single man. On the morning of that very day, because Chen Mingchu was brought to justice, he was the first to be killed in revenge; called out by name and dragged forth, he came back no more.

For my own part I thought that the men of No. 76, having taken so heavy a blow, could not but mean revenge; at that time both Chengwo and Yu Yanzhi had already had word of their coming release, and their cases were not grave, but, reckoning by circumstance and by standing, it seemed to me that I might well become the target of their revenge. I said then to Chengwo that I would surely be shot; Chengwo asked me for what reason, and when I told him, he still comforted me. So I wrote two letters beforehand, and entrusted them to a fellow-prisoner in the same room whose political case was simpler, and portioned out all my clothes and things, and waited quietly for death, to repay the nation! Little did I dream that at half past four that same afternoon Chengwo and Yanzhi, the two of them, would be called out and killed—it was truly as a thunderclap from a clear sky, and startled the whole roomful of us! After the two of them had gone out of the room, we stared dumbstruck and could not swallow even our supper; a grieving air hung over the whole room, and in every man there was a nameless grief and rage.

At the moment Chengwo's name was called, he was lying on his bed, just wakened from his noon nap, and I sat on my bed writing my autobiography, when of a sudden came a sound of footsteps, and someone shouted: "Zhu Chengwo! Yu Yanzhi!" With the buttons of his cotton gown not even fastened, and Yu Yanzhi close at his heels, he strode out after the warder who opened the door. We thought then that he and Yu Yanzhi were being called out to be talked with, or else were being released, and as they left we even blessed them, saying that this time they went out to freedom. But when they had gone out the door, we saw through the window that the hands of both Chengwo and Yanzhi were cuffed behind them, and that many onlookers stood in the yard—and only then did we know the thing was gravely amiss! Our hearts sank on the instant; Xu Zhan, Tang Yadong, and I, the three of us, looked at one another and could not speak, and the taste in every heart was truly beyond telling, grief and rage woven together, as we watched the two of them stride off toward another world! We too were prisoners awaiting execution—what remedy had we? Yu Yanzhi I did not know well; I knew only that his surname had been Chu, but his given name I did not know. With Zhu Chengwo I had of late grown very close, and understood much of his character and his learning; I held him truly a man of ability, and that he should be killed thus, though it be called dying for righteousness in the nation's cause, was after all a loss to the nation and to the organization. So on the day of his martyrdom (the twenty-fifth of the twelfth month of the twenty-eighth year, five in the afternoon), I made an elegiac couplet to mourn him, and the lines were:

You served the state with loyalty and faith; and now, when these embroidered rivers and hills lie broken, of a sudden you have given your body to make good your benevolence—shame on me, left to die after you. / You kept in your house the filial and the brotherly way; yet, while but an aged mother and weak sisters barely survived, you laid down your life and laid hold on righteousness—I mourn you, and your whole life long.

The author of the above text, Mr. Xu Wenqi, was mentioned in this book's first chapter, third section, in that little passage on "assistant secretaries," where it was written: "The comrades who served as assistant secretaries were many; when the writer took over there were Yi Zhen, Hu Shangwu, Xu Wenqi, and others …" Mr. Xu says he worked at the head office at No. 104 Aitang Road; the head office may have been the district office of the "Shanghai District," and the district office kept its work in several places. The first place I went to when I took over was Avenue du Roi Albert in the French Concession; whether I ever met Mr. Xu face to face, think as I may, I cannot recall. Mr. Xu says he was captured at the end of the tenth month of the same year; I wrote to Brother Zheng Xiuyuan to ask about this, and Brother Xiuyuan told me over the telephone that he too could not remember clearly. Still, Brother Xiuyuan recalls that after the victory in the War of Resistance he met with Xu Wenqi at Nanjing, and that afterward Xu went off to America.

Of the two comrades Tang Yadong and Xu Zhan, shut up with him in Xu's account, Brother Zheng Xiuyuan's "True Record of Three Perils on the Shanghai Shore" says: "The Third Brigade's commander Tang Yadong and deputy commander Xu Zhan both came to Taiwan; Brother Tang served in the industrial-and-mining police corps, and died of illness in Taiwan in his early years. Brother Xu served for years in the Central Printing Works." The Jiang Anhua who was Third Brigade commander in the first section above must have been Tang's successor.

Xu's account mentions too the killing of the martyr Zhou Xiliang. As to the martyr Zhou Xiliang's origin and deeds, the writer inquired of the quarters concerned, and was told there was no record to be traced; and asking further among friends and fellows, all likewise said they did not know the man. So it seems that Zhou Xiliang very likely used an alias. Beyond this, only in the "Original Text of the Grounds of Judgment on the Traitor Ding Mocun," printed on a newspaper cutting that Mr. Xu Shouyan sent me (with no paper's name and no date, but reckoned to be of the thirty-sixth year), is there a line: "The courier Zhou Xiliang, for stealing important documents, was shot on the twenty-seventh of the twelfth month of the same year." The "Zhou Xiliang" used here differs from Xu's "Zhou Xiliang" by the middle character, near in sound though not the same in the writing; and his day of martyrdom, by Xu's account, should be the morning of the twenty-fifth of the twelfth month of the twenty-eighth year. This martyr Zhou Xiliang was truly a "nameless hero."

Of the martyr Yu Yanzhi's personnel record, too, there is nothing. For this the writer inquired of Brother Zheng Xiuyuan, former secretary of the "Shanghai District," who told me: Comrade Yu Yanzhi may have been transferred from the "Loyal Army" side, but the rest he no longer remembered. Only in another official document did I first find such words as "Fifth Action Brigade commander Yu Yanzhi." Now, in this book's first chapter, in the brief notice of the "Fifth Action Brigade," the writer said: "With this brigade I was truly too little acquainted; I recall only that its earlier commander was Wang Fuqian, alias Wang Yang, whom we never once had contact with; later Wang Fuqian came to grief and was captured …" Then—was this commander Wang Fuqian, who came to grief and was captured, the same as Yu Yanzhi? To prove this point, so slight a reference alone would not do; some strong ground must be found. Presently Brother Liu Yuanshen told me to my face: "The Fifth Action Brigade commander Yu Yanzhi I have an impression of, only I never met him face to face. His coming to grief and capture, and his cruel killing, was not long after the 'July Fourteenth' incident of the twenty-eighth year; at that time all the comrades of the 'Shanghai District,' inner and field alike, had scattered and gone into hiding for safety's sake, and word no longer passed freely, so that the course of Comrade Yu Yanzhi's sacrifice cannot be known in detail. As for the later Fifth Brigade commander Wang Fuqian, alias Wang Yang, that was his true name; he had once hung out a shingle as a lawyer in Shanghai, and his capture was a thing of the early spring of the thirtieth year of the Republic—nearly two years, that is, after Yu Yanzhi gave his life. I myself was captured on Avenue Joffre in the French Concession on the twenty-eighth of the sixth month of the thirtieth year, and, delivered by the Japanese Hongkou gendarmerie on to No. 76, was shut in one great cell with Wang Fuqian, who by then had been captured several months before me. So Yu Yanzhi and Wang Fuqian are not one man; in fact Wang was Yu's successor." This, of course, is the most reliable proof, and the doubt of before was thereby cut through at a stroke.

The martyr Xu Shouxin (alias Zhu Chengwo), when he died for his cause in the twenty-eighth year of the Republic, was but twenty-nine years old. Before he joined the work of the "Juntong Bureau," he had served as chief foreman of the telecommunications department of the Central News Agency. After joining the work in the twenty-sixth year, he was posted chief of the head radio-station at Yuanling, and afterward transferred to Guiyang, still as chief of the head station. In the seventh month of the twenty-eighth year, when the "Shanghai District" met with mishap several times over, the chief communications inspector Yang Zhenyi was thus exchanged with Xu Shouxin.

Brother Yang Zhenyi later served as deputy director of the Investigation Bureau of the Ministry of Justice and Administration, and died of illness some years ago; while Mr. Xu Shouxin died young for his cause. The lots that life allots differ each from each—this is what is meant by "seeking benevolence and finding it," and there is no dividing it into fortunate and unfortunate.

In a corner of the cutting, Ding Mocun has a passage of pleading bearing on the matter, whereby he shoves off, clean and clear, an atrocity of a thousand unpardonable evils. Ding argued speciously that he had been forced to join No. 76, having neither fist nor courage, that the real power lay wholly in the hands of Wu Shibao and the rest, and that he himself was under control—let alone the killing of men. That he could bring himself, brazen and shameless, to say such words!

Touching the killing of the men of resolve, in the "Original Text of the Grounds of Judgment on Ding Mocun" there is, in proof, a telegram of the former National Government's Bureau of Investigation and Statistics of the Military Affairs Commission (that is, the "Juntong Bureau"), dated the twenty-second of the tenth month of the thirty-fifth year of the Republic, Jing-Zhen-Hu No. 4731. Its facts are as follows:

"Xu Ke, a member of the First Intelligence Group among the underground workers of the Shanghai District of the former Military Affairs Commission's Bureau of Investigation and Statistics, was shot dead in Shanghai on the twenty-fourth of the fifth month of the twenty-eighth year of the Republic; Li Chuchen, leader of the Fifth Intelligence Group, was captured after a failed attempt to sanction Ding Mocun and Li Shiqun in Shanghai, and was killed on the twenty-fifth of the second month of the same year; Chen Zhaoqing, a member of the Fifth Intelligence Group, was captured after a failed sanction of Li Shiqun, and was killed on the twenty-fifth of the second month of the same year; the communications inspector Xu Shouxin, for reporting to the Center, was killed on the twenty-seventh of the twelfth month of the twenty-eighth year; the Fifth Action Brigade commander Yu Yanzhi, for the secret keeping of arms, was killed on the twenty-seventh of the twelfth month of the same year; the courier Zhou Xiliang, for stealing important documents, was shot on the twenty-seventh of the twelfth month of the same year; the directly-attached courier Xu Amei was likewise shot in the course of the twelfth month of the same year; Peng Furong, captured for carrying out an action case in Shanghai, was killed on the thirteenth of the fourth month of the same year. These eight members were all seized and killed by the puppet Special Operations Headquarters (No. 76); the Central workers listed above as having perished were all cruelly killed within the period when the accused (Ding Mocun) served as director of the puppet Special Operations Headquarters, and the accused must bear the whole responsibility."

The eight martyrs named in this original text of the grounds of judgment were all working comrades of the "Juntong Bureau."
