Of them, three—Xu Shouxin (alias Zhu Chengwo), Yu Yanzhi (perhaps an alias, the true name known only to be surnamed Chu), and Zhou Xiliang (also written with a different middle character)—have been recorded before; but of the five martyrs Xu Ke, Li Chuchen, Chen Zhaoqing, Xu Amei, and Peng Furong, though the cutting here and there gives group and title, no personnel record of them can be found—and this is the very reason the heroes are nameless.

In the above original text of the grounds of judgment, the date of the martyrdom of the three—Zhou Xiliang, Xu Shouxin, and Yu Yanzhi—was not the twenty-seventh of the twelfth month, but should be the twenty-fifth of the twelfth month. I here set it right.

Furthermore, the working comrades of the "Juntong Bureau" who died in the demons' den of "No. 76" during the War of Resistance, from the twenty-eighth year down to the eve of victory in the thirty-fourth, were of course not merely the eight listed above.

In the early part of the twenty-ninth year, the "Shanghai District" drew up a "Plan for Striking the Enemy," proposing to its superiors that, within a fixed region and under certain conditions, it be allowed to deal at its own discretion with, and to shoot down, armed Japanese officers and men, with no need of prior report. After this proposal was sent up, it was some months before the order came down granting leave to carry it out. In the course of the Bureau's work this was, though a first venture, a new departure withal; and in the pages of the history of the War of Resistance, too, it ought to hold a place.

This case, from the day it began to be carried out—the twenty-ninth of the ninth month of the twenty-ninth year—down to the twenty-second of the tenth month of the thirtieth year, saw, by the statistics our side openly published, upward of sixty-odd Japanese officers killed or wounded in all; while by the scattered records our side has on file, and by work-reports that cannot be verified, the figure went far beyond this number. And as to its actual effect: the killing and wounding in quantity could, to be sure, sap the strength of a strong foe, and a sweeping momentum was enough besides to chill the gall of the Japanese bandits.

Among the deeds of enemy-slaying above, one Japanese of no little power at that time, named Akagi Chikayuki, was also done away with by the "Second Action Brigade" belonging to our "Shanghai District." Akagi Chikayuki's title was deputy commissioner of police of the International Settlement's Municipal Council—that is, the highest man of the Japanese side taking part in the police administration of the International Settlement.

Though this man held no soldier's rank, yet in that setting, to have had the power to bring down a Japanese deputy commissioner of police—what a mark would that not set up? And the more so since he was the very foe with whom we were locked hand to hand.

The whole warp and weft of the case is described as snugly as thread meeting thread; the source of the material is a short passage from the Japanese-language internal publication "A True Record of the Mainland Gendarmerie." In truth, the author of that piece was himself a party to the case.

The youthful patriotic body that had grown up and waxed great at Tianjin, its deeds shining bright—the "Anti-Japanese Traitor-Killing Corps"—from the latter half of the twenty-ninth year onward saw a number of its cadres and members come, one after another, to Shanghai, and thereupon throw themselves into the ranks of the anti-Japanese traitor-killing. Their fighting spirit ran high, their momentum was in full flush; they asked no title and drew no pay, seeking only to lop off a few more heads of the Japanese dwarf-bandits, to wipe out the shame of the nation and the race and to avenge its wrongs, careless though it should cost their very lives.
Truly, the "Kang Corps" comrades in Shanghai sought benevolence and found it, and made the greatest of offerings and sacrifices!

A passage at the close of the third chapter above mentioned that, after the "Shanghai District" had sanctioned the two traitors Chen Mingchu and He Xingjian, the comrades, in their grief, feeling that all this was an evil seed sown by the Japanese warlords, put a concrete proposal to their superiors: its main purport was to ask their superiors' authorization to deal the armed Japanese officers and men of the Shanghai region a stern blow, killing them without quarter. The original proposal held these three main points:

One: to take Japanese soldiers in uniform as the objects of the killing—whatever the height of their rank or the size of their office, with no need of prior sanction or report—and, once the chance was got, to do away with them on the spot.
Two: the place of execution to be limited to the zones the Japanese army occupied and the bounds of its sphere of power.
Three: so far as might be, to avoid bringing harm upon the safety of our own country's inhabitants.
To make it easier to understand, and to answer some doubts that might arise, I set forth these three points again as follows:

Before the "Shanghai District" put forward this proposal, by the rules, to sanction anyone at all, the enemy's forces included, one had first to have sanction from above; but this case set a special precedent—that one might act as convenience allowed, striking first and reporting after—and in fact it could not be otherwise. Consider: from outward appearance we could at most tell only the arm of service and the rank of a Japanese soldier, and could never learn his post or his name, for they wore, one and all, no badge or nameplate. As to what task he bore, that was less to be known still. And the more so since such affairs befell, for the most part, in the moment of a chance encounter.

Worth a special mention here is the motive of this undertaking: the chief reason we wished to kill Japanese soldiers with our own hands was righteous indignation—one might say, a hatred struck alive by the cruelty and inhumanity of the Japanese army. All our countrymen who lived through those eight years of calamity, if they be not too forgetful, must find the memory fresh still and the after-pain lingering; and we, who were locked hand to hand with the enemy in unceasing struggle, had of course a hatred more of the flesh. The reaction in the minds of the common run of comrades then was this: if, without prior sanction, one might straightway kill armed Japanese officers and men, they would all, vying to be first, gladly carry out this task.

To kill Japanese officers and men in uniform was the same as attacking the enemy on the field of battle: it aimed to strike at the enemy's morale and to wipe out the enemy's strength, and cared not, of course, whether he were Zhang the Third or Li the Fourth. The reason we did not kill those in plain clothes was that, even knowing him for certain to be a Japanese soldier, we regarded him as "disarmed." If a day should come when Japanese soldiers dared not stalk about everywhere in uniform, preying upon our countrymen, that would prove this action had told.

Now for the limiting of the place of execution: Shanghai was of a special kind because of the foreign Concessions there. Though the "Concessions" were Chinese territory, they were under foreign rule. The Japanese army at that time had occupied only the outer region of Shanghai, the so-called Chinese quarter; but toward the International Settlement, led chiefly by Britain (and taking in America, Japan, and others besides), and the French Concession, held by France alone, it still kept things as they were. As for the Japanese power's pressing into the two Concessions, that was a thing after the Pearl Harbor affair.

Before the Pearl Harbor affair of the eighth of December, the thirtieth year of the Republic, the range of the Japanese army's activity, apart from the belt round about Shanghai, was centered on Hongkou. "Hongkou" was a part of the International Settlement; the Japanese had managed this patch of ground for a long while past, and their chief military and civil organs were all set up there, and it was on the streets of Hongkou that Japanese officers and men came and went the most. Besides this, in the extra-Settlement road districts of western Shanghai in the International Settlement, traces of Japanese troops were now and again to be seen. Armed Japanese soldiers appeared too, on occasion, in the International Settlement and the French Concession, but few in number, and mostly along the Bund by the banks of the Whangpoo.

The reason we were unwilling to carry it out within the Concessions was that we had need to use the Concessions for cover; and next, to avoid drawing upon our government a diplomatic reproach from the Concession authorities. One might say it was somewhat a case of sparing the rat for fear of the vase. In truth, as later proved, all these misgivings were needless.

As for the bringing of harm upon the local inhabitants—that is, the harming of our own innocent countrymen through the killing of Japanese soldiers—this had been seen again and again in the past: after every action or act of sabotage the Japanese army would seal off the scene and arrest the nearby inhabitants at will, and, besides severe torture, would plunder, ravish, and do every evil at their pleasure. In places near the great cities, where eyes and ears were many, they might still show a little scruple; but in the poor and out-of-the-way villages, there they did as they pleased the more. To give a real instance: in the spring of the twenty-seventh year, in the case where the writer, at Beiping, led Wang Wen and other comrades in person to sanction the puppet chieftain of the first rank, Wang Kemin, the Japanese military at once, afterward, sealed the nine city gates, cut off all coming and going, and in the space of one night made a great, all-out search, arresting more than three thousand men in all—of whom only the two, Wu Hanqing and his wife, had any connection with us. The rest all suffered the calamity of the fish in the pond. Warned by this, we admonished our comrades earnestly: never beforehand to use the inhabitants' houses for shelter, and afterward to withdraw from the scene as far as might be, and on no account, for a moment's safety, to enter a dwelling and hide. In other words: rather run a little more danger than drag in our countrymen. After the "Shanghai District" put this proposal to its superiors in the early part of the twenty-ninth year, four or five months passed before the order of approval came down. In that interval, our superiors must have given the matter careful thought. If not that, then it was that the Bureau, too, dared not take much upon itself, and went again to ask the highest levels. Because there was no precedent, whether it might be done thus the highest levels would of course weigh in full, to avoid a gain not worth the loss. Large as the "Shanghai District" was, it was but one field unit of the Juntong Bureau, and it was truly not for it to guess much at the nation's policy-making.

After the "Shanghai District" received the superiors' telegraphed order granting the request, it did not issue a general order for all its brigades and groups to carry it out alike, but gave the charge, selectively, only to a few action units. Why? Reason one: besides this, we had much other work to do, and could not all of us do this one thing alone. Reason two: it had to suit the particular capacities of each field unit, for some units were not fitted for it. Reason three: as said above, since there was no precedent, what would the effect be after it was carried out? and how would every quarter respond to it? One had first to listen and to look, so that, if anything were amiss, it might be set right in time. Earlier, in framing this proposal, I had separately exchanged views on the workability of the idea with my schoolfellow Jiang Anhua, commander of the "Third Action Brigade," and Comrade Bi Gaokui, leader of "New Group One"; both held it full of meaning and well worth a trial—that in the carrying-out it was no hard thing, and that, small in sacrifice and great in power, it was a stirring both to our comrades and, above all, to the hearts of the people in the fallen zone. That being so, when the task was given out, these two units were the first to be chosen. Afterward, the "Second Action Brigade" and the "Sixth Action Brigade" were added, one after the other.

The killing of Japanese officers and men began in the ninth month of the twenty-ninth year and came to a stage's end in the last third of the tenth month of the thirtieth year; in that one year and two months, some fifty-odd cases in all of Japanese soldiers killed or wounded, the dead and wounded together above sixty in number. The figures listed above are but rough, for the years are long past, and to set them out one by one with name and surname is no longer possible; even were all the files turned over, they could hardly be traced out. In memory, there were all sorts, from private soldiers up to commissioned officers, the highest in rank a major-general.

At that time, after every shooting of the enemy's troops, it was only in the news reports that one might learn the name of the man struck, and mostly it was a surname without a given name. As to the height of rank, the enemy's side kept it deep secret and made no public announcement. There were cases, too, kept wholly secret, of which the news breathed not a word, so that who the dead or the wounded was, was never known at all.
Here I have gathered several news reports; though but a few lines each, they were not easily come by, and read today, they must carry a taste all their own.

(One) The Chongqing Ta Kung Pao of the seventh of the tenth month, the twenty-ninth year: "Central News Agency, Hong Kong, telegram of the sixth—Shanghai dispatch: about nine in the morning of the sixth, an enemy gendarme, riding a bicycle, was of a sudden fired upon before the Zikawei Cathedral; a bullet struck him in the back, and, wounded, he fell to the ground. The enemy gendarmes stationed at the Communications Mansion, and the puppet police, hurried up at the word, sent the wounded gendarme back to hospital for treatment, and mounted a guard nearby and made a search, with no result whatever."

The writer is not too familiar with the streets of Shanghai; if I am not mistaken, "Zikawei" is at the border of Fahua township of Shanghai and the French Concession, while within the French Concession there is besides a "Route de Zikawei." Since enemy gendarmes and puppet police hurried up at the word, the place where the affair occurred ought to have been in the so-called "Chinese quarter" of the Shanghai city; had it been within the bounds of the Concessions, there would have been no enemy-puppet gendarmes or police. Still, the French Concession too had its extra-Concession roads—could it have been on that stretch of extra-Concession road?
Though the report above does not point it out clearly, yet had he not been in uniform, how could one be sure the wounded man was a Japanese gendarme?
This wounded Japanese gendarme—who he was, we never knew; still less do we remember which unit it was that did it.

(Two) The Chongqing Ta Kung Pao of the sixteenth of the twelfth month, the twenty-ninth year: "Central News Agency, Hong Kong, telegram of the fifteenth—Shanghai dispatch: at eight in the morning of the thirteenth, in Hongkou there befell again a case of the sniping of an enemy officer. Four assassins broke into the residence of Major Kubota of an enemy special-service organ on Dixwell Road and fired at him, but Kubota, dodging, was not hit. Enemy troops and police hurried up at the word and seized three of the assassins."

Now the Japanese military organs were for the most part in Hongkou, and the "special-service organs" of every kind and every strangeness were the more full of tricks and turns; which "special-service organ" it was is truly hard for the moment to make out. What office this Major Kubota, who was not hit, filled, cannot be made clear either. As for the seizing of three "assassins," they were of course all action men of the "Shanghai District." By the look of the news above, it should have been a planned deed, and it stands better to reason than a thing done on a sudden whim. Then, since a plan had been drawn up beforehand, and afterward three comrades were captured, the writer ought surely to have some impression of it—how is it that not a bit of it will come back to me?

According to the record in the "Table of Cases Committed by the Blue Shirt Society in Shanghai," printed in the Shanghai Sin Shun Pao of the twenty-eighth of the eleventh month of the thirtieth year, the Kubota case fell on the thirtieth of the eleventh month of the twenty-ninth year, at Seward Road in Hongkou; time and place are both unlike, and only in this are they the same—that the man struck, Kubota, was unhurt. And of Japanese surnamed Kubota there was, of course, more than one, so that whether this was one affair or two cannot be made out.

In the Ta Kung Pao's report it is "Major Kubota"; in the Sin Shun Pao's table no rank is given, but in the table's last column, "the action man"—that is, the unit that carried it out—it is noted: "Third Brigade, Jiang Anhua and Lin Huanyao." Setting these side by side, one may hazard a rough supposition: the case was one that Commander Jiang Anhua of the "Third Action Brigade of the Shanghai District" sent Lin Huanyao and other comrades to carry out, which failed for not striking the target man Kubota. Afterward, unable to get away in time, three were captured on the spot; as to who those captured were, and whether Comrade Lin Huanyao was among them—since my schoolfellow Jiang Anhua has been dead these many years, it can no longer be traced.

Bound up with the affair above is another piece of news: "Central News Agency, Hong Kong, telegram of the fifteenth, Shanghai dispatch: the enemy on the fourteenth opened the western-Shanghai blockade zone; the reasons, it is heard, were two. First: the gambling dens on Great Western Road and Yuyuan Road, the Hualo Restaurant and the like, being unable to do business under the blockade, suffered no small loss, and so with a great sum bought the road open, the amount in all five hundred thousand yuan. Second: the enemy held that the search for the so-called terrorists need not be spread so wide, and so opened the outer part, but Wangjialong and such places were still under blockade."

Now the Kubota case fell in Hongkou in the northern quarter, and the enemy troops, to search out our working comrades, blockaded even the whole stretch of western Shanghai. Here we may take two views of the Japanese army: one, that the matter was grave, as though a great foe were upon them; the other, that they were fierce of face and faint of heart, overwrought beyond measure. And this too was just as we had foreseen at the first—that after every case of a Japanese soldier shot, the most luckless afterward were still the local inhabitants, and of them, of course, our Chinese countrymen the most.

(Three) The Shanghai Chung Mei Jih Pao of the twenty-third of the twelfth month, the twenty-ninth year, reported, from this paper's own dispatch: "Late the night before last, about eleven, a Japanese consulate policeman named Miyazaki Satoshi, thirty-two years of age, for reasons unknown, was hacked and wounded with wild blows of a blade near Wenmiao Road in Nanshi, and fell prone in a pool of blood; presently the police-station car carried him to the International Relief Association in the refugee district for treatment, but at last, from too great a loss of blood, he died soon after reaching the hospital. Afterward the Japanese gendarmerie made investigation on the spot, with no result whatever."

The affair of the Japanese policeman Miyazaki Satoshi, killed by grievous wounds, is recorded too in the so-called "Table of Cases Committed by the Blue Shirt Society in Shanghai": the time the twenty-second of the twelfth month of the twenty-ninth year, the place Wenmiao Road in Nanshi, the unit that carried it out the "Third Action Brigade" under Jiang Anhua's command. Set side by side with the particulars printed in the Chung Mei Jih Pao, all agrees very closely.

"Nanshi" is in the southern quarter of Shanghai, not a Concession. The "police station" in the report should be the puppet police bureau. The "International Relief Association of the refugee district" was, one supposes, a charitable body. This case won no encouragement from our superiors, for the spirit of it lay in striking at armed Japanese officers and men, and a Japanese policeman, though he wore a uniform, was after all no soldier; so that, strictly speaking, to do this was truly not right. Examining again the cause of the error, it may be that the action men were not clear in telling apart their dress.
There is one phrase in the report rather full of meaning, and that is "for reasons unknown"! What better explanation could there be, save the gift of war?

(Four) The Chongqing Ta Kung Pao of the fourth of the first month, the thirtieth year of the Republic, a Central News Agency Shanghai dispatch of the third by way of United Press, headed: "Gunfire on the Solitary Island—Another Enemy Soldier Dead." It said, on reliable word: "The Japanese soldier Takahashi was, on the first, in the central quarter of Shanghai, stabbed to death by an assassin of unknown name. This is the fifteenth Japanese army man killed in Shanghai since the twenty-ninth of the ninth month of last year."

According to the record in the so-called "Table of Cases Committed by the Blue Shirt Society in Shanghai": "Takahashi Katsuharu, on the first of the first month of the thirtieth year, was struck and wounded near Jiangwan; the action man, Third Brigade, Jiang Anhua."

No question, this is of course the same affair; the differences are these—here a surname without a given name, there both name and surname; here dead, there wounded; here in the central quarter, there at Jiangwan—and whether Jiangwan counts as the central quarter depends on which angle one takes for a starting-point. Suppose one take, for the center-point, the International Settlement and the French Concession that lie side by side: to the west is "western Shanghai," most of that quarter extra-Concession roads; to the south a great tract called "Nanshi," the old city quarter of Shanghai; to the east, commonly called "Pudong," parted off by the one Whangpoo River; to the north, called "Zhabei," taking in Hongkou and Jiangwan. This is the outline of the whole of Greater Shanghai. Whether this account can give the reader a notion of it, I do not know. Worth marking is this report of United Press, which says: "This is the fifteenth Japanese army man killed in Shanghai since the twenty-ninth of the ninth month of last year." How is this to be explained? After looking into the materials bearing on it, I found that the truth was this—

According to what the Shanghai Chung Hua Jih Pao carried, our action of killing Japanese officers and men began on the twenty-ninth of the ninth month of the twenty-ninth year: the first case was the killing of the Japanese soldier Isobe Yoshie, the place the corner of North Sichuan Road and Wuchang Road; the second was carried out on the thirtieth of the ninth month, and killed the Japanese soldier Satō Seiichi, the place Zhenning Road in western Shanghai. Of what rank these two were, none knows; only that it was Third Brigade, Jiang Anhua and his men, who did it.

As to whether, by the time it came to this case of the Japanese soldier Takahashi Katsuharu, he was already the fifteenth, that cannot be traced out. Still, that they reported it so, they must have had some ground in the materials.

(Five) The Shanghai Shun Pao of the sixteenth of the first month, the thirtieth year of the Republic, printed: "It is rumored that near the Japanese naval drill-ground eight bombs were found. According to what a certain English evening paper carried yesterday—that the Japanese naval landing force had found eight bombs on Kungping Road—the reporter has heard from a police officer of the Wayside Station in that district that the thing is not exact; the truth being that at the time a Jewish child picked up there one old-style hand grenade, carried it home, and it was then sent on by his family to the station to report."

The same Shun Pao said further: "The English Shanghai Evening Post and Mercury says: the Japanese naval landing force, yesterday afternoon (the fourteenth), found eight bombs in a ruined house next to the Japanese naval drill-ground on Kungping Road, and the landing-force soldiers contrived to remove them. When this news first got out, it was commonly mistaken that these bombs had been set there beforehand by terrorists, meaning to blow up and harm the Japanese troops. At present the Japanese side is making investigation, to determine the actual source of these explosives."

Just so—these could only be called "explosives," and not "bombs," for they were all demolition devices of differing shapes, made to suit the setting so that on the outside one could not tell what manner of thing they were. These were designed and put together by the comrades of "New Group One" themselves; perhaps because the level of skill had not yet reached its full heat, none of them "went off."

The aim of "New Group One" was to blow up the Japanese naval landing force; quite true, just so—they had set these "explosives" beforehand in a ruined house near the drill-ground, some of them with a "timing device," some "contact"-fused. The first thought was to set them off when the Japanese naval landing force was at drill, and so deal a heavy killing; and for fear the force of them was not enough, they laid several down at once—whether it was the "eight" said, I cannot recall the number clearly. It may be, as the report says, that a child playing in the ruined house carried home one of these "explosives" he could make nothing of. If that were so, then perhaps it was because the time had not come that it did not go off.
The world is full of chance coincidences; but by the demands of our work, this must of course be counted a failure.

(Six) The Chongqing Ta Kung Pao of the tenth of the fifth month, the thirtieth year: "Central News Agency, Hong Kong, telegram of the fourth, Shanghai dispatch: at the puppet Central Market, guarded by the enemy, a Japanese inspector was shot dead; afterward the enemy seized several tens of innocent vegetable-sellers, and made a house-to-house search near Sinza Bridge and other places, so that for days on end trade at the puppet market was quite deserted."

Again: "Central News Agency, Hong Kong, telegram of the fifth; the Sin Wen Pao carried: yesterday the Japanese troops made a great search in Zhabei and arrested more than five hundred inhabitants. According to inhabitants who were released, the Japanese troops held several photographs, and, unable to make an arrest and break the case, arrested every man of suspicious movement in the whole district and checked them one by one against the photographs, with the result that not one man was alike."
The dead man's name could not be traced, nor his exact standing made out; the report says only "a Japanese inspector," who was very likely one in uniform.

What must be pointed out here is the search and the arrests afterward: first, several tens of vegetable-sellers of the market were seized, and then, in the great search, more than five hundred nearby inhabitants were arrested. Whence the Japanese troops got those few photographs, none knows; and they checked, one by one, among these five hundred and more—lucky it was that none matched, for had there truly been a few "alike," those would have died with no ground to be buried in.

These six cases above were all found in newspapers of more than forty years ago; a pity it is that there was no way to get whole copies of those old papers of the day, and so no systematic and exact account could be made.

In the writer's impression, the fruits of all the "Shanghai District's" enemy-slaying actions were surely more than this number; but to list them out one by one, no reliable material bearing on it can for the moment be found, and so I let it be.

In sum, the "enemy-slaying item" the "Shanghai District" carried out did in those days truly shake the Japanese garrison of the Shanghai region; the plainest fact of it was that for a long stretch of time uniformed Japanese soldiers, save that they went in company and on their guard with one another, never dared walk the roads singly, one by one; the glaring of eyes and the forcing into people's houses at will grew rare; and that overbearing, world-defying arrogance of theirs was not what it had been before. This, we hold, was the effect struck out by our blows. As for the great gladness in the hearts of the people of the fallen zone, that goes without saying.

At the end of the seventieth year of the Republic, the writer met at Taipei with Mr. Ōtsuka Kiyoshi—who during the War of Resistance had been chief of the Special Higher Section of the Nanjing "Gendarmerie Command" under the "General Headquarters of the China Expeditionary Army," and who afterward, through several promotions, was transferred again to head some department of the "Military Affairs Bureau" of the Japanese Army Ministry. He gave me in person a few photostatted pages of "A True Record of the Mainland Gendarmerie," without head or tail, so that one could not tell when it was published—perhaps an internal publication, not issued abroad? I do not know Japanese, and, having leafed it over, put it away. Not long ago I had it translated and looked at it: the chief content of these few pages was a writing of our "Shanghai District's" anti-Japanese actions during the War of Resistance.

Among them one long passage described just the course of how we planned to do away with Akagi Chikayuki, deputy commissioner of police of the Municipal Council of the Shanghai International Settlement, and the actual state of things at the scene of the deed. Now I excerpt below the record in "A True Record of the Mainland Gendarmerie," true to its meaning. Only, some of the terms and names in it, which looked not quite right, I have set straight.

This piece bears no author's signature, and is in the first person; by its tone and its content, it may have been written by an officer or non-commissioned officer of the "Shanghai Japanese Gendarmerie." Its meaning ran as follows:

"Before we were dispatched to our posts, we had already heard that the Chongqing underground workers then in Shanghai were extremely active. Toward Japan and toward the new Nanjing regime headed by Wang Jingwei, they took a most severe policy of burning and killing, and plots of this sort went on without cease. The shooting, on the seventeenth of June, on Yuyuan Road in western Shanghai, of Mr. Akagi Chikayuki—deputy commissioner and special police superintendent of the Police Department of the International Settlement's Municipal Council, dispatched by the Japanese Ministry of Foreign Affairs—was one such case.

"Mr. Akagi Chikayuki held the real power of police affairs in the Municipal Council of the Shanghai International Settlement, and was at that time a man of weight in the balance. The course of his being sniped was thus—

"There was a constable named Li Dechang, his constable's number 3332, who, from the twenty-first of February of the sixth year of Shōwa (the twentieth year of the Republic) until his dismissal on the seventeenth of January of the sixteenth year of Shōwa—in near ten years of service—had, in the tenth month of the fifteenth year of Shōwa, singlehandedly seized two armed robbers robbing a Chinese shop on Sinza Road in the International Settlement, and won a second-class police medal. In his twenty-eighth year, because he kept a tryst with the woman constable Fang Huisheng, whom he loved, and did not find anyone to stand in for his duty, he was dismissed on the ground of absence from post.

"After Li Dechang was dismissed, he drifted about for some months, until, on the sixteenth of May of the same year, he was actually recruited by Li Zhengliang, leader of the third group of the Blue Shirt Society's action brigade, and its deputy leader Ye Dongshan, and secretly joined their work. Li Dechang at once furnished the intelligence that deputy commissioner Akagi Chikayuki lived on Yuyuan Road in western Shanghai.

"Li Zhengliang, alias Li Liang, was, after graduating from the Chongqing special training class, dispatched to Shanghai to work. On the twelfth of November of the fifteenth year of Shōwa, he had shot dead, at the Great China Hotel on Yu Qiaqing Road, the Taiwanese Lin Zijiong, a 'director of the China Workers' Welfare Association' who aided the Japanese side. Li Zhengliang was twenty-six, a man of Anhui, and a fierce anti-Japanese element.

"Ye Dongshan, twenty-eight years of age, a man of Shandong, alias Ye Dong. In December of the year before last he joined the Blue Shirt Society in Shanghai, using the post of headwaiter at the Great China Hotel as cover. On the thirtieth of January this year he shot dead the pro-Japanese Chinese Li Xiangqing, and again on the fourteenth of March shot dead the pro-Japanese Chinese Pan Shudong and one other, two men. Ye Dongshan's elder brother Ye Yusi is at present a sub-inspector in the narcotics-suppression department of the Seventh Section (Criminal Section) of the Police Department of the International Settlement.

"Li Zhengliang, Ye Dongshan, Li Dechang, and the rest all belonged under the Third Action Brigade commander Jiang Anhua. This Jiang was a colonel out of the engineering course of the Whampoa Military Academy, at present in hiding within the Shanghai Concessions, directing his more than fifty subordinates in action work.
"At that time they were all under the command of the Blue Shirt Society's Shanghai District chief Chen Gongshu, and took their orders directly from Chongqing.

"The plot to assassinate deputy commissioner Akagi began on the first of June; over some ten days' work, each day the exact times of the deputy commissioner's going out to duty and returning home, and the routes he passed by, and so forth, were recorded. At the same time, from eight each morning, when he left home for work, until half past nine at night, men kept up a watch near his residence. They had at first set the eleventh of June to seize the chance and act, but were forced to break it off because it happened to rain. So they changed it again to the fourteenth of June, to carry out the original plan, but unlooked-for, just at that moment there chanced to be taxis blocking before and behind Akagi's car, and for want of a clear stroke it was again called off. Thus at last, on the morning of the seventeenth of June, group leader Li Zhengliang ordered deputy leader Ye Dongshan to lead the four—Li Dechang (the constable, dismissed and turned informer, of the earlier record), Zhou Zhenfang (a laborer, newly joined a month before), Yu Senlin (a textile-factory worker, newly joined), and Yang Jingwen (formerly company commander of the seventh company of the second battalion of the Jiangsu Peace Preservation Corps on the Chongqing side)—to set out from Kiaochow Road, and by way of Jinjiaxiang to reach Jessfield Road in western Shanghai, disposing each man's place as follows: Li Dechang, who knew the deputy commissioner by sight, was the first marksman, standing in wait in secret with a large Mauser pistol at the corner of Yuyuan Road and Tifeng Road; Yang Jingwen, at the southeast turning of Tifeng Road, pushed a flat-board handcart heaped with odds and ends, playing the part of a transport coolie, to push it out in good time and block the car's advance the moment Akagi's car passed; and Zhou Zhenfang and Yu Senlin, the two of them, each holding a revolver, stood quietly across from Yang Jingwen, charged with the sniping; while Ye Dongshan, the scene commander, was posted on Yuyuan Road, whence all could be overlooked, to patrol and watch.
The original text notes—there is besides a sketch-map of the scene appended for reference, here omitted.

"At fifty minutes past eight in the morning the disposition was complete; at fifteen minutes past nine, Li Dechang made out the deputy commissioner Akagi, come out together with his wife, driving swiftly up in his car, and at once gave the signal by shaking his hat. Yang Jingwen, taking his meaning, swiftly pushed that handcart out and blocked the deputy commissioner's way to good effect; almost at the same instant, Yu Senlin and Zhou Zhenfang drove forward a few steps, and Yu first fired at the driver, meaning to make it so the car could not be driven off, and then pressed up to the half-open right-side window and fired at Akagi; but because the wife, seated on the right, held Akagi tight like a shield to shield her husband, though three bullets were fired, none struck Akagi in a vital spot. At this moment the other marksman, Zhou Zhenfang, also fired two shots, neither hitting. In an instant, just as the deputy commissioner Akagi, with his right hand, flung open the car door meaning to run out, Yu Senlin, pistol in hand, reached in through the window and with one shot struck him in the chest; yet the commissioner, wounded, rolled out under the car and grappled hand to hand with Yu Senlin, until, his strength spent, he fell at last to the ground. Seeing this, they all withdrew swiftly and scattered by the appointed routes. At this moment Li Dechang fired a few more shots, but only for cover before the retreat.

"In an instant, the western-Shanghai special police hurried up at the word, and Yu Senlin, who had grappled with Akagi, was, for drawing back a little late, taken on the spot, and one pistol given up. This gun was an American-made .38-caliber revolver, its number 51524.
"As for the deputy commissioner Akagi, gravely wounded and fallen, he was already past all calling back to life.

"This case was handled jointly by the Police Department of the International Settlement's Municipal Council together with the Shanghai Japanese Gendarmerie; those taking part were Assistant Commissioner of Police Nakamura Tsuneo, Superintendent Kobayashi Minesaburō, sub-inspector Sugimoto Kisaburō, and others, working in concert with the men of the 'China Squad' under Major Ōtsuka Kiyoshi and Warrant Officer Katōda and below, under the command of Lieutenant-Colonel Hayashi Hidezumi, chief of the Special Higher Section of the gendarmerie's Shanghai headquarters, to carry out a large-scale round-up against the Blue Shirt Society's Shanghai District.

"Four months later, come the twelfth of October, they at last seized the whole sixty-odd, from the Third Brigade commander, Colonel Jiang Anhua, on down. Only Li Dechang, one man, was of unknown whereabouts; though traced to his native place, Qingjiang, nothing was got of him. His sweetheart Fang Huisheng was of unknown whereabouts too.

"This affair gave us a lesson: being a deputy commissioner of police, he yet lived at that time in the dangerous district of western Shanghai, and carried no gun on him besides—this perhaps a common failing of the Japanese. And the more so since he hired a man for a driver, and did not understand the need to change his driving route often."

The reason this passage in "A True Record of the Mainland Gendarmerie" is written so full and so deep is, on the one hand, that he must have been a party to the case—possibly Ōtsuka Kiyoshi himself; and on the other, that he plainly gathered the confessions of those captured.
When the writer had read it, it drew up not a few memories, and stirred some reflections too; I set them down below as they bear on this case, not straying too far from the theme:

At that time—that is, the twenty-eighth and twenty-ninth years—our "Shanghai District's" understanding of the "Japanese Gendarmerie," and theirs of our "Shanghai District," were about equal. For instance, we knew only that the "Japanese Gendarmerie's" Special Higher Section chief was surnamed Lin, but did not know his full name was Hayashi Hidezumi; and they, for their part, wrote the shu of Chen Gongshu's name with the "tree" radical, as a different character. And, for another instance, they called our "Juntong Bureau" the "Blue Shirt Society" all along, while we too never came to know clear and whole the inner workings and division of labor of their Japanese Gendarmerie. These are all facts there is no reproaching, and there is no need to cover them over. From this one may draw a principle: that when two hostile sides each seek to understand the other, it is impossible to have it all at one's fingertips. Even if inside lines are laid, there is but a difference of degree.
Next, to review again the content of this record:

We find that the Japanese gendarmes, even before they had reached their post—Shanghai—already harbored dread of our "Juntong Bureau's" activity behind enemy lines. Were we alone to say so, one might mistake it for magnifying our words in self-praise; but coming from their own mouths, it may too be seen how far our "power" then reached, and that it did indeed work a considerable effect.

The Li Zhengliang mentioned in that piece—his true name was Li Liang; he had trained in the Bureau's Qianyang training class, and after being sent to Shanghai I assigned him to the "Third Action Brigade" as leader of the "Fourth Group," to be Commander Jiang Anhua's aid, meaning besides to foster him and, watching how he did, to give him heavier charge. A pity it is that he was captured in the tenth month of the thirtieth year; in my memory it seems he was not seized by the "Shanghai Japanese Gendarmerie" but fell into the hands of "No. 76." Though he was the director of the Akagi Chikayuki case, yet he was not "handed over" to the gendarmerie to "answer the case," nor was he "put to death" by the enemy and the puppets for it.

As for the comrades Li Dechang, Ye Dongshan, Zhou Zhenfang, Yu Senlin, and Yang Jingwen, of their deeds and of their life or death I truly cannot say. Now Jiang Anhua and Li Liang have both been dead these many years, and in the long-dust-sealed files their connected records may not be found either; so the more is it worth setting down here.

By the record in "A True Record of the Mainland Gendarmerie," the beforehand disposition of the Akagi Chikayuki case, and the course of the struggle on the spot, are all worthy of marking and of praise, showing forth in full not only the wisdom and boldness of our comrades but also, plainly, how the sons and daughters of China looked on the enemy as a foe.

The commander Jiang Anhua and many below him were indeed captured one after another in the months following the case, the time about the ninth month to the middle of the tenth month of the thirtieth year; but it was not, as the Japanese Gendarmerie says, that they broke the case—in fact it was still "No. 76" that sold their souls. And by reference again to what the Chung Hua Jih Pao carried, after the sixteenth of the ninth month of the thirtieth year there was indeed no more news of the Third Brigade going out to strike at the Japanese. To sum up: all the comrades of the "Third Action Brigade" under Jiang Anhua, in the "enemy-slaying" actions, carried out more than twenty cases in all, and killed or wounded more than thirty Japanese officers and men; weighed against the working setting of that day, to call it "a brilliant record of arms" would be no excess! And all of it, of course, was got in exchange for their blood and their lives.

After the commander Jiang Anhua was seized by "No. 76," was he ever delivered to the "Shanghai Japanese Gendarmerie" to be questioned or confronted with his case? At the time I saw no report of it, and now I cannot recall; but that he did not "perish" then is a fact. The pity is that in the spring of the thirty-fourth year, on his way back to the great rear, passing a "checkpoint," he was actually done to death by treachery; the inside of it is most tangled, and to this day it cannot be made sure at whose hand he died his unjust death.

Then again, on the "Shanghai Japanese Gendarmerie's" side, from this account it is not hard to find that they always have somewhat of exaggeration and of claiming merit. Most grievous of all is that, had our own personnel-organization not been too little tight, they would surely have been no match for us; for we were hidden, and resistant, and one in hatred of the foe, while they were ever on the defensive, like a rat crossing the street.

All that is listed above is but a part of the "Shanghai District's" action work in this period; and before the month of July there were yet more records.

The White Russian Ivanov, sanctioned in the French Concession on the fourteenth, was the very faithless wretch who sold out the martyr Chen Sancai. The martyr Chen Sancai was a man of key connection in the plan to be rid of Wang.

During the War of Resistance, in the fallen zones, the war zones, and the great rear alike, there arose many patriotic bodies of youth; though their backgrounds differed and their names were various, in this alone were they wholly the same—the ardor to resist Japan and requite the nation. The "Anti-Japanese Traitor-Killing Corps" here recorded was one such.

If to say this "Anti-Japanese Traitor-Killing Corps" was unlike the rest should smack of favoring the one over the others, or of old Wang praising his own melons, and even draw reproach—yet if I make a brief and plain report, unadorned, of the heroic sacrifice and the valiant deeds of the "Anti-Japanese Traitor-Killing Corps," then, once all have understood, they cannot but exalt their greatness.

First one point must be declared: touching the birth and the growth of the "Anti-Japanese Traitor-Killing Corps," in the "Biography of Mr. Dai Yunong" and the "Complete Works of Mr. Dai Yunong" there are long passages of record; yet these are but foil-work, not enough to express the corps' basic spirit, nor bringing out where its essence lies. Such a saying as "the Kang Corps was a peripheral instrument used by the Juntong Bureau"—for this I truly cry injustice on behalf of the Kang Corps comrades.

By reason and by fact alike, the "Juntong Bureau" and the government organs stand for the nation; the "Anti-Japanese Traitor-Killing Corps" was a patriotic body of youth, belonging among the people's associations. The making of the relation between them rested on the guiding line that patriotic youth had need of the nation to resist the outer aggression; while for the government's part it lay in adding a measure of resisting strength. In this there was no so-called dividing of "core" and "periphery." And the more so since these young students had no title—they were, first and last, but corps members; nor did they draw pay, and what they used in their activity was all the snack-money their families gave them. This was in nature wholly unlike the intelligence lines the "Juntong Bureau" employed; how, then, could it be looked at so narrowly? Mr. Dai Yunong was of grand talent and large design; he could rein in a million men, but would never confine himself to a self-centered "intelligence viewpoint." If he has knowledge in the world below, I believe he would surely not be pleased to have his biography set down its pen so.

To put it honestly from yet another angle: the birth of the "Anti-Japanese Traitor-Killing Corps" and its being had their own objective setting and background of the age, and were by no means made out of nothing by any one man's single hand. Though the "Juntong Bureau" gained by the Kang Corps' outstanding showing, this—besides the effort of Comrade Zeng Che in the work—was for the greater half a blessing sent down by Heaven too.

The reason the writer dares so to word it is just that this patriotic body of youth was born in that period when I served as chief of the "Tianjin Station" and held besides the post of deputy commander-in-chief of the "North China Loyal and Patriotic Army," soon renamed the "Luan-Yu Guerrilla General Headquarters." (What was first written was "formed by my own aid"; thinking it over again, I felt it unfitting, and so amended it as above.) And why do I say unfitting? This is no false modesty: for at that time I had two great distractions abroad—first, the "struggle for power" with others in the military activity; and second, a "going off the rails" in my private conduct of life. So many affairs I entrusted to Comrade Zeng Che to do for me. In the very winter of the twenty-sixth year, once Zeng Che made a verbal report to me, saying he meant to take part in a "youth activity," and I just nodded my assent; as to what manner of "youth activity" it was, I did not much understand. Only afterward, in order to gather a body of youth to join the ranks of the "Luan-Yu Guerrillas," did I come to heed this matter.

Let me begin, from what I know, with the conceiving of the "Anti-Japanese Traitor-Killing Corps." In the twenty-fourth or twenty-fifth year, it is said, a body of young students of Tianjin went to Baoding for joint training; and during that training, some of them formed a connection with the political body of that day, the "Renaissance Society" (see the first chapter of "Rooting Out Traitors in the North"). Whether the seed was thus sown, I dare not say for certain, but there was some measure of a bond in it.

When the "Double Seventh" affair at the Marco Polo Bridge arose, the students in schools of middle grade and above at Tianjin at once fermented the organizing of anti-Japanese bodies, whence came the founding of the "Tianjin Youth National-Salvation League." Those Comrade Zeng Che, then secretary of the "Tianjin Station," came into contact with were just these people.

To take a further part in the actual activity of the War of Resistance, the active elements in the "Tianjin Youth National-Salvation League," with Comrade Zeng Che's encouragement, formed the ever-imperishable "Anti-Japanese Traitor-Killing Corps."

Whether the name of this patriotic body of youth—the "Anti-Japanese Traitor-Killing Corps"—was proposed by the "Tianjin Station" of that day, and then put forward by Zeng Che and acknowledged by all, my memory is now blurred.

The founders of the "Anti-Japanese Traitor-Killing Corps," it is learned, were Li Baoqi, Shen Dong, Guo Zhaohe, Li Rupeng, Li Shiren, Chen Zhaoji, Zeng Che, and others, with Li Baoqi as "the eldest" and Zeng Che ranking second. This too I heard only lately; whether it is so, it is said besides that a certain Mr. Sun, at present a delegate to the National Assembly, knows in more detail.

In the course of its growth, over the question of the working line, differing opinions arose within the "Kang Corps": some held for the tongue's and the pen's assault, laying weight on cultural propaganda; others would have nothing but real blade and real gun, a fight to the death; and so each put forth his own strength, and each afterward had his own indelible achievement.

What the writer saw was this: those of the quieter sort dipped into their own pockets, bought paper, borrowed a mimeograph, pasted up anti-Japanese slogans and scattered anti-Japanese handbills, and for a time made the Tianjin city quarter—the Japanese Concession within it included—wondrously lively, so that even the constables could not arrest them all, showing forth in full the nation's ardor against aggression.

Among the action-eager group, vying to be first to kill a few Japanese with their own hands, one band led by Chen Zhaoji, with Zeng Che for go-between, joined the cadre training class run by the "Luan-Yu Headquarters," and after a month set out to wage guerrilla war in Baodi County in East Hebei. When these twenty-odd men held their training-opening muster on the upper floor of a school, I once gave them a talk; present too were Wang Tianmu, Wang Wen, Zeng Che, and others.

Another band, fierce for hard doing, the action faction, formed of themselves a five-man executive council, with Li Rupeng over organization, Sun Dacheng over action, Zhu Zongliang over technique, Yuan Junhan over general affairs, and Zeng Che over liaison and coordination. The arms they needed were the one problem they could not settle for themselves, and that had to be supported by the "Tianjin Station." These patriotic youths, nineteen in number, were all middle-school students still in school, who, save in the cinema, had never so much as seen a real gun, let alone how to handle one in the hand. Consider: placed in that setting of the day, where all was under restriction, unable to find a place to shoot at a target or to fire live rounds in some hidden spot, they could at most only strike a pose and go through the motions. Even so, once they set one off in play; luckily it was a fright without harm, and drew down no disaster.

In truth, only let there be a breast full of hot blood, and matchless courage arises of itself; a small thing like not knowing how to fire a gun could by no means stop their onward march, and could as well accomplish the heroic feat of sanctioning traitors.

In the two years from the twenty-seventh to the twenty-ninth, the action and sabotage work led by the "Kang Corps'" five-man executive council carried out many cases. On the Tianjin side, such as the puppet Hebei provincial education-department head Tao Shangming, the puppet Tianjin chamber-of-commerce chairman Wang Zhulin, and the puppet Tianjin customs superintendent and puppet Reserve Bank general manager Cheng Xigeng—all were the corps' doing. On the Beiping side, too, there was the puppet Construction General-Administration general-affairs bureau head Yu Dachun and many more. The most strategically valuable of the sabotage work was the burning, three times over, in three warehouses at Tianjin, of more than ten thousand bales of cotton the enemy troops had scraped together and were waiting to ship. That a band of young students, untrained, and no more than eighteen or nineteen years of age, could do such earth-shaking great things is truly a rare thing indeed!

The enemy were no dead men, and of course would not wait to be beaten and not strike back. Anytime and anywhere they sought their chance, and struck back without cease. By the reckoning: the "Kang Corps" comrades, since throwing themselves into the anti-Japanese traitor-killing work, came to grief nineteen times in all, and eighty-three were captured; the dead were Zeng Che, Feng Yunxiu, Li Rupeng, Ji Shuren, Ji Nianhua, Zhu Yun, Chen Weilin, Yuan Hanjun, Li Xin, Huang Kezhong (in another record named Huang Ruitang), Miao Wei, and others—a dozen and more. These are those whose names are known; besides, of those whose names are unknown or whose whereabouts are lost, there were many more.

Now to tell: after Comrade Zeng Che and the rest came to grief and were captured, the "Kang Corps" did not for that stop its activity. That Comrade Sun Dacheng who headed the action work, having luckily escaped peril, came again to Beiping. He lay under cover in a school, still seeking a line, meaning to accomplish the unfinished task—to carry out the sanction of the number-one economic traitor of North China, Wang Shiying (see the sixth chapter of "Rooting Out Traitors in the North"). Before long, unlooked-for, plainclothes Japanese gendarmes tracked him down, and seeing there was truly no staying, he made his roundabout way at last to Qinhuangdao. Here, much by the help of the family of one Kang Corps comrade, who at the risk of danger got him a "Kailan Coal Mines" staff certificate, he took a collier first to Shanghai, and then by way of Zhejiang, Jiangxi, Hunan, and Guizhou went to Chongqing. This was a thing of the third or fourth month of the twenty-ninth year. At that moment, though I was in Shanghai, we were not in contact.

Of the "Kang Corps'" further activity in the Beiping-Tianjin region I know still less, so I stop here, and go on next to tell of Sun Dacheng after he reached Chongqing, and how he came again to Shanghai.

Sun Dacheng saw Mr. Dai at Chongqing; besides comforting and encouraging him much, Mr. Dai still hoped he could go back to Tianjin and go on leading the "Kang Corps'" work. Sun gladly accepted; only, there was one great problem that could not be settled—that there was no way to warrant surely breaking through the Tianjin blockade line and getting safely into the city. Later, Mr. Dai, after much thought, asked Dacheng's mind again: was he willing to go to Shanghai?

Comrade Sun Dacheng reached Shanghai on the eighth of the seventh month of the twenty-ninth year, his standing that of a representative of the "Anti-Japanese Traitor-Killing Corps." The "Kang Corps" was not a working unit under the "Shanghai District"; it kept still its own distinct style as a patriotic body of youth. But Shanghai was not the birthplace of the "Kang Corps," and of course it could not turn about there as at Tianjin, so that in many things it needed the "Shanghai District's" guidance too.

After Sun Dacheng reached Shanghai, we met once and settled all such matters as courier and liaison; afterward it was given over to the assistant secretary Brother Liu Yuanshen to take direct charge of liaison and guidance. As for the support the "Shanghai District" gave, it was but three hundred and seventy yuan of fabi a month, and nothing else was asked. And this figure, from the ninth month of the twenty-ninth year down to the tenth month of the thirtieth, was never once raised.

Thereafter the "Kang Corps" comrades reached Shanghai one after another; those who lodged with Sun Dacheng were the three—Qian Zhilun, Ye Yichang, and Liu Shihua. Others, such as the comrades He Minxin, Kan Jinwan, and the rest, were scattered in many places, all keeping a "single-line" contact with Sun Dacheng. Just for this reason, whenever a mishap befell, save for the little unit that came to grief, there was no wider entanglement. This too was a great feature that the Shanghai "Kang Corps" bred, drawing on the Tianjin experience.

The "Shanghai District" itself had many action units; the upshot of our coordination was to decide that the "Kang Corps" should not do action work, but bend itself to propaganda, sabotage, and disturbance. So the "Kang Corps" in Shanghai never carried arms. As for the demolition stores they needed, at first the "Shanghai District's" "Technical Room" supplied them, and later they made their own and used their own. This was another feature of theirs.

The "Kang Corps" comrades transferred from elsewhere to Shanghai, one after another, numbered about not more than thirty; yet they took on besides, on the spot, thirty or forty men, so that at the most they were near seventy in all. Though their number grew little by little, they could still keep their old quality, and, like before, their fighting spirit ran high and their momentum was in full flush; what was theirs alone, held within their breasts, was but the one loyal heart of anti-Japanese traitor-killing.

Sun Dacheng first rented a shop-front house on Park Road, opening the Fusheng Water-and-Electric Firm for cover, and could also use this place to store some "raw materials" and "tools." Afterward, through a stretch of preparation, he threw himself into it with utter disregard of self.

At first, it may be that these pure and guileless patriotic youths could not abide the drunken-gold, dazzle-paper luxury of the Shanghai Concessions, and that those who came and went in such places were mostly a set of Wang-puppet upstarts; so once, on the Christmas Eve of the twenty-ninth year, they on the one hand sent men to paste up anti-Japanese handbills in great quantity along Nanking Road and other bustling streets, and at the same time set explosives in five or six dance halls, whose killing power, as made, was not strong, meaning only to give warning. Unlooked-for, when the time came they all went off, and it is said one man died and many were wounded—which was beyond what was at first reckoned. Reviewing it afterward, I for my part hold that this way of doing, though its spirit is to be praised, is not to be encouraged; its greatest fault was that there was no fixed target.

On the sixteenth of the fourth month of the thirtieth year, three Shanghai "Kang Corps" comrades—Luo Changguang, Liu Shihua, and Huang Kezhong—after several observations, found that at the two cinemas on Chapoo Road and Haining Road in the Hongkou district all who went in and out were Japanese, among them uniformed Japanese soldiers too; and so, their motive stirred, after some planning, they made ready to blow it to flinders. It is not known where they got the dress and the props; disguised as workers delivering bottled drinks, they seized the chance to mingle into these two cinemas, set two timed demolition devices severally at the foot of the wall in the dark, and withdrew safely. When the hour came, the two theaters sounded off together, and this thing was, after all, done clean and neat.

Afterward the Japanese side called this affair the "Tōwa Theater Calamity." As it happened, one of the two theaters was named "Tōkō" and one "Yūwa," so together they were called "Tōwa." According to what the Japanese side let out, in this one affair there were twenty-three casualties in all, every one of them Japanese, among them several Japanese gendarmes. Whether there was besides a high Japanese officer among them is not known.

This thing, looked at from the angle of two nations at war, was done and done; there was of course nothing that might not be, and to have the chance to give them a lesson was fitting in the extreme. Set beside the "Nanjing Massacre" or the "dropping of the atom bombs on Nagasaki and Hiroshima," it was the more a trifling thing.

On the second of June and the twenty-sixth of July of the thirtieth year, the Kang Corps comrades twice over wrecked the Japanese-run "Hetong Department Store" on Route Massenet in the French Concession, doing the company considerable harm, and the second time more fiercely than the first. Here I would say a word not too grave: they did this kind of thing as though finishing it were mere play.

On the eleventh of June of the thirtieth year, the Shanghai "Kang Corps" comrades did a "drawing a tooth from the tiger's mouth." On Route Père Robert in the French Concession there had been a dormitory of the Mitsui Company, later taken over by the "French Concession gendarmerie detachment of the Shanghai Japanese Gendarmerie." That night the "Kang Corps" sent out three men—Li Xin, Sun Kemin, and Liu Shihua—who, in the deep of the night's dark, slipped past the sentries, one man climbing the wall while two kept watch and stood ready, set a timed explosive at the foot of the window, and withdrew again by the way they came, and were lucky to complete the placing. Do not think, told so, that it was simple; to do it was no trifling play, and once a slip befell, it would be past bearing. Who knows how great a courage it must take!
The upshot of this case: several rooms of the dormitory were blown up, and one Japanese gendarme gravely wounded—but the Japanese side declared him "unhurt."

In the sixth month of the thirtieth year, reconnaissance found that the enemy troops often used the open ground within Hongkou Park to muster and give speeches, to drill and exercise, and now and again a man of higher rank came there to hold a review. The Shanghai "Kang Corps" chief Sun Dacheng held it a fine chance, and drew up a plan to send out two men, Miao Wei and Huang Kezhong (also named Huang Ruitang), who first won over, near Hongkou Park, the man of a "cigarette kiosk" (a small standalone wooden hut), and began to carry the demolition stores over by turns, to be stored beforehand, ready to be placed when the deed was to be done. For fear of the inconvenience of carrying, and to dodge inspection and other mishaps that might befall, this should have been the most thorough scheme; yet unlooked-for a grave misfortune befell all the same!

By the record, it says: "Just as they were about to dash forward and throw, because the enemy troops' guard was strict and the action had to be especially swift, in the flurry the bomb, unhappily, went off by mishap, so that the two comrades Huang and Miao gave their lives heroically on the spot."

In the twelfth month of the seventy-second year, the writer met for a small gathering with my young brother Sun Dacheng, and we spoke too of fragments of this affair, laying weight on just how the mishap came about. By Dacheng's recollection, how exactly the thing went wrong he cannot, even now, come to a sure conclusion on. That is to say: was it that in the assembling he carelessly set it off himself? Or that on the way into Hongkou Park it went off by mischance, through friction or a knock? Or was it, too, possible that, before they could place the "demolition device" they held in hand, they were found out, and, in the surge of shared hatred of the foe, set it off on purpose, seeking to perish together with the enemy? Whence would come the "several enemy sentries wounded and killed at the same time" of the record.

Following this, to probe a layer deeper: suppose it went off by mischance in the very course of assembling—then the "cigarette kiosk" they borrowed must have been damaged, plain for all to see afterward, self-evident and needing no more inference. If, after it was assembled, the two, carrying the demolition device, set it off unwittingly on the way into Hongkou Park—then it would have blown up only themselves, and there would not have been the fact of several enemy troops wounded and killed at once. But if it went off only after they had placed it in the park—then the two comrades Miao and Huang could have withdrawn safely to their ranks, and would not have been blown to bits and sacrificed. So it is said: the likeliest part is that they set it off themselves and perished together with the enemy.

On the first of August of the thirtieth year, through Japan's threading of the needle, Germany, Italy, and several other nations gave the Wang puppet regime diplomatic recognition; and the Wang puppets, in the flush of favor, held "lantern-parade celebration rallies" at Nanjing, Shanghai, Hangzhou, and other places. The "Kang Corps" comrades, hearing of it, were greatly angered, and, to make plain the nation's justice and guard the nation's dignity, held it must be punished. After conferring, they resolved to send three comrades—Li Xin, Zhang Zhonghua (also named Zhang Zhixin), and Huang Kun—bearing home-made bombs, to the rally-ground at Jessfield Park in western Shanghai, to disturb and wreck it. Here the files hold a passage of record, whose gist is: "Some held that the rally-ground was thronged and mixed, easy to enter but liable to be blocked on withdrawing; and the more so since, throwing at the moment of setting off, in the press of the crowd one might often fail to throw it out, or, thrown not far, it would burst—and if so, one could hardly avoid harming oneself, and must take care. Comrade Li Xin declared with feeling: 'At the rally the enemy and puppet chief men are all gathered; though I myself be not spared, it is no more than three men, and if by seizing this chance I can wipe out the whole pack of bandits at a stroke, how could I let it slip by?' Those who heard were moved to solemn awe, and the two comrades Zhang and Huang too declared themselves willing, with the resolve of certain death, to lend their strength shoulder to shoulder, and so went forth in high heart."

And sure enough, the rally was thrown into commotion by the sound of the blast, and those attending ran off scattering like birds and beasts; but our good brother—Comrade Li Xin—actually perished together with his bomb, and gave his life on the spot. By what my young brother Dacheng told me to my face: "Some of our men saw that at the time Comrade Li Xin, though blown so that his belly burst and his bowels streamed, at his last gasp, still cried out 'Long live the Republic of China!' without cease." How heroic! how bitter!

At the scene of the mishap, Comrade Zhang Zhonghua, unable to get away in time, was captured, and Comrade Huang Kun was lost in the confusion; what was the fate of the captured? had the lost one any whereabouts? that I do not know—let me ask my young brother Sun Dacheng again, and if there is material, supply it later.
Afterward, in the news the Japanese side put out, they listed the end of the disturbing of the "celebration rally" as a "self-destruction."

On the twenty-ninth of August of the thirtieth year, the Shanghai "Kang Corps," nowise cast down by two mishaps, pressed on again and, at No. 321 Foochow Road in the International Settlement and at two places in Hongkou at once, burned down the main store and the branch of the "Santong Book Company," which dealt solely in enemy and puppet books and periodicals, so that it could not open for business for a long while.

On the fourteenth of October of the thirtieth year, my young brother Sun Dacheng, through a mishap in developing a demolition agent, unhappily blew off one arm; but he did not mind, and it was with the other arm that he served the nation these forty years and more, and to this day he is still at his post. Most to be revered is that, over these decades, never once has he been heard to speak a word of complaint.

Now to tell how his arm was blown off: because in the two blasts at Hongkou Park and Jessfield Park comrades had been sacrificed—though not necessarily through the poor quality of the explosives—yet he was ever minded to develop a more finely-wrought "product," to meet a wide need. When he had put it together, by the procedure it had to "pass a test-blast" before he dared use it with an easy mind, so he took a small packet (a lump) and laid it on the tram rails, to see whether it would go off under a hard pressure. Unlooked-for, when tried it did not work; and he did not let it be at that, but took the thing up in his hand again and fiddled with it—and just at this moment, with a sudden crack it burst, and he fainted away; when he woke, he was already lying in the prisoners' ward of the Guangci Hospital. Captured together with him were the two comrades Qian Zhilun and Ye Yichang.

By the eighth of December, the Pearl Harbor affair, the Japanese troops pressed into the French Concession, and the three comrades Sun, Qian, and Ye were at the same time delivered from the hospital to the headquarters of the Hongkou Japanese Gendarmerie; luckily it was not made out what they did. Though they tasted torment of every kind, they kept their lives after all. Were one to ask how they came back from hell to the world of the living, that would be a most tortuous tale of wonder. It is too long to tell; let me settle it in a word—they were "worked" out at a price by the wife of that Mr. Lu ——, whom our "Shanghai District" had, on the thirteenth of June of the twenty-ninth year, opposite the Kwang Hua Theater on Avenue Edward VII, sanctioned and wounded but not killed, a woman all called "Godmother Lu." Why did she do it? Here again, how am I fitly to answer?

After Sun Dacheng and the rest were captured, the "Kang Corps'" activity in Shanghai did not break off, but went on, headed severally by Zhu Zongliang, Yuan Hanjun, Lü Naihao, Liu Shihua, and others, as lively as at the first. Only, before the victory they still came to grief many times, with sacrifice again and again.
At present, the footprints of the "Kang Corps" folk are spread over the whole world, in every stratum of society; they are, forever, of the very best.

What the writer takes for his boundless regret is truly that what he knows is not complete enough, and in the matter of deeds there must be omissions; and, out of regard for the safety of the comrades caught fast on the mainland, he dares not speak all his mind out to the full.

The "tycoon" was a man of a special sort, having wealth and power, that arose only in the Shanghai Concessions of about the twenties. Had there been no foreign Concessions on Chinese soil, this breed of men would never have appeared.
This breed of men stood for the latent forces of a deformed society; and, to speak of their root nature alone, good and evil were out of all proportion.

The Shanghai-bred "Concession tycoon" differed from the foreign article, the "underworld boss": the "underworld boss" made his sole business of crime and villainy, and cared only for gain; the "Concession tycoon" had already come into his own, and, besides gain, angled besides for name and fame, and in the showing of his conduct strove hard for the upper current—yet who knows whether their hands were washed clean or no?

Zhang Xiaolin was just such a "Concession tycoon"; in his day of favor, though it could not be said he called up wind and rain, yet he too did as he pleased, and was truly in his glory for a good long while. After the War of Resistance broke out, because there was proof of his communicating with the enemy, and he would not heed the government's counsel to leave Shanghai, the order came down to sanction him.

The "Shanghai District," ordered to carry out this case, had the "Second Action Brigade" report that it had already got an inside lead, only lacking the man's surname. Within a month, by the fourteenth of the tenth month of the twenty-ninth year, Zhang Xiaolin was, sure enough, shot dead by a bodyguard he himself had hired, on the upper floor of his own house.

On the very night of the affair, the Second Brigade, in its written report, first named the executioner Lin Huaibu. The "Shanghai District," having reported it on, presently received a telegram of commendation, and so it became a settled case. In the decades since, no man has ever doubted it.

When the writer lately re-checked the old draft, because his subjective wishes had faded, the more did he feel there were many doubtful points in the case, such as: that beforehand the executing unit did not, by the rules, report to the district and set on record the name of the inside-line man it had arranged; that afterward, when Lin Huaibu was captured and held in the French police station, whether that brigade ever had contact with him—of this there is no sequel; and that after the victory in the War of Resistance, it was rumored that Lin Huaibu had been released from prison, but the several units under the "Juntong Bureau" never knew, first to last, who had ever seen this man—let alone of placing him anywhere.

Did Lin Huaibu shoot Zhang Xiaolin dead out of a moment's passion? or was it a planned deed after receiving an order? none dares say for sure. If it was planned, is it to be supposed he never thought he could not get away afterward? And if he had already held the resolve of certain death, then why need he wait until he had been struck before he acted?
